#2062. 'I feel betrayed, misled, in shock. It was a stupid thing for them to do': ANDY WOODMAN relives the moment he was 'brutally' sacked by Bromley - and how his best mate Sir Gareth Southgate helped him cope

Published: 21:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 05:29 EST, 11 November 2026

Every sacked manager has a sob story – but few dismissals have felt as harsh as Bromley’s recent decision to part ways with Andy Woodman.

Pound for pound, no club has outperformed their history, budget and expectations in English football across the last decade as much as Bromley. But after an understandably tricky start in League One – two wins from their first 10 games – Woodman was shown the door.

In his first interview since that decision last month, the 55-year-old tells Daily Mail Sport about feelings of 'betrayal' and 'shock' before making his pitch to future employers. But the most eye-opening part of our candid conversation comes when I ask the man with more than four decades of experience to recall the club he took over in 2021.

‘Look, Bromley is your classic non-League club,’ says Woodman. ‘I mean that with the greatest respect to all non-League clubs and I hate the word “non-League” as I think it should be “League Three”, as they are all professional.

‘But the facilities are non-League, the mentality is non-League. Everything is done day-to-day, hand-to-mouth, every penny counts, every decision that costs money counts, it is run by people’s personal money.

‘It was tough when I started: we had no turnstiles, no club shop, we trained on the pitch because it was astroturf, we had no gym.’

Andy Woodman was sacked as Bromley boss last month despite leading the club to the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season

Woodman with the FA Trophy in 2022. 'Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair,' says the former Bromley boss

Under chairman Robin Stanton-Gleaves, Woodman and Co, Bromley changed this mentality and shot up the pyramid, winning the FA Trophy in 2022, promotion to the Football League in 2024 and then another promotion to League One last season. Two months later, it was all over.

Asked how he feels about the decision, Woodman, who used to coach in the Arsenal academy system, says: ‘Yeah, I feel betrayed. Every manager who gets sacked, we all have a story of hardship to tell and all feel it is unfair. That’s fine, I get how the football business works.

‘But the bit that didn't sit comfortably with me was the conversations I was having with people at the club or owners, everyone above me… there was no inkling of any of this. I feel misled. I was surprised.

‘One day, we were talking about plans and the way forward and how to get through this sticky little period with players out injured, then the next minute it was a change of direction. Nothing like, “Right, you’ve got three games to turn it round”, none of that, nothing.

‘My record was good there, the owner always said if anyone can churn out results it was myself. Football has no patience. In football, people always forget where they come from. I understand wanting to move forward. It’s disappointing really, that’s the best word I can use. I feel let down.

‘It was just a normal day when they told me. I was going into training, popped across to where the chairman’s office was and then was just told, “We are going to take a change of direction”. It was no more than that, I didn’t try to change the decision or ask why.

‘It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is… I am sure people will read this and think, “You deserve this” and “You deserve that” but what else can you do? There’s no easy way of doing it.

'When you have been told you are sacked, you don’t really want to stick around and have a long conversation. They didn’t give an explanation. They needed results, they said. We lost to Leicester which was not a great result, obviously. But realistically they are Leicester… and we are Bromley.’

'It was a two-minute conversation, it didn’t need more than that really. I went to tell the staff and went home! It sounds brutal and it is'

Woodman, who used to be the Arsenal youth team goalkeeping coach, says: 'When I left Bromley that day, I just felt in shock to be really honest'

To hammer home that last point: Woodman’s first game was against Wealdstone in April 2021 in the National League at Hayes Lane. On that same weekend, Leicester were hosting soon-to-be champions Manchester City. Oh, and the Foxes won the FA Cup a month later.

‘When I left that day, I just felt in shock to be honest,’ continues Woodman. ‘I felt the next three games were winnable. I had played seven of the top 10 teams, beaten the top team Huddersfield, my goalie was just coming back from injury and some others were coming back.

‘We had two teams in the bottom four and one just outside so I felt it was my best opportunity to get some much-needed results.

‘To take someone out who has been in football 40 years and been in coaching 25 years and then to put (his former assistant) Byron Webster in charge who had just been fresh out of playing and has never done a coaching session… with every respect, it feels unfair to him. It was a stupid thing to do. I found that really strange, they took one point from those three games. It fascinates me.’

Now, with Bromley bottom of League One, Karl Robinson, the former Salford and MK Dons boss, has taken over. Woodman, though, is keen not to sound bitter and will remember his five-and-a-half years at the club with fondness. He says his best memories are taking Bromley into the Football League, playing at Newcastle in the FA Cup and beating ‘Hollywood Netflix club Wrexham’ in the FA Trophy final.

Sir Gareth Southgate remains his best friend, the pair having met as teenagers in the Crystal Palace academy. They took turns in being best man at each other’s wedding and Southgate is godfather of goalkeeper Andy’s son Freddie, who is on Liverpool’s books.

They also co-authored the 2004 book Woody and Nord which chronicles two polar opposite career paths that started at the same level, one going on to play (and later manage) England, the other a journeyman in the lower leagues.

‘Nothing surprises Gareth and I,’ adds Woodman. ‘We have been in the game for 40 years now. You can argue that in his tenure at England, he got them as high as they have ever been in 60 years and it still was not enough. So it doesn’t surprise us. People have to make decisions and they are business-related, only time will tell if it is the right decision but that’s not my problem any more.

Woodman and lifelong friend Sir Gareth Southgate at the release of their 2004 book 'Woody and Nord' which charts two very different careers in football

Southgate is godfather to Woodman's son Freddie, a goalkeeper on Liverpool's books

‘Gareth was very supportive, so was Alan Pardew and the support from the Premier League right down to the National League, there has been no end of messages I have had, which is comforting.

‘That first Saturday after being out, I didn’t want to be watching or listening to the game, I just wanted to get away because that is the worst. I have had two clubs ring me, there are ongoing conversations and I am just making sure it is the right vehicle for me. What I mean by that is I want an owner that is aligned and who thinks they can compete to get out of their league.

‘My record speaks for itself. If you ask most managers how many promotions and trophies they have won, I bet over long careers, they haven’t got many. For me, with the smallest budget in the leagues, we maximised the team and maximised success.

‘To get two promotions and an FA Trophy win against Wrexham, hitting the play-offs four times in five years, that is something I am really proud of. If nothing else, the Bromley supporters and town are grateful.’

#2061. Arsenal Women vs London City Lionesses preview: Gunners face tough test at the Emirates

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal look to build on their recent win over Liverpool as they return to the Emirates Stadium but will face an impressive London City Lionesses side who are a potent attacking threat on their travels.

Renée Slegers’ team have struggled to convert their strong performances into points in the league this season. They have lost their last four WSL games at home, however, becoming the first team in WSL history to draw four successive games at home.

Their bad run must come to an end. They have taken just three points from their first nine league games so far this season, scoring a miserable total of 10 goals. However, they look like they have more in the tank and will need to be much more clinical in front of the goal.

The day also marks Slegers’ 50th game in charge of the WSL. The Dutch manager has only lost six league games so far this season, with only Chelsea having a better record from teams that have been ever-present in the division.

Arsenal can’t take their opposition lightly after London City’s impressive recent form. They have won two and drawn once in their last three away league games, scoring 12 goals.

Eder Maestre’s side has become a potent attacking force. Daniëlle van de Donk has provided four assists this season, and Delphine Cascarino has scored three goals and provided two assists.

Kadidiatou Diani can be dangerous. She has scored or assisted in all four of her league games away from home this season.

London City’s attacking prowess means they are a far different proposition to some teams Arsenal have faced at home. They have been in a positive situation for 62.7 per cent of their league minutes this season, the highest in the WSL.

Arsenal will have to deal with the attacking threats but look to utilise their ball possession better. Giving London City an opportunity to counter could make an already tough afternoon even tougher.

Alessia Russo comes into the game having found the net in her last three WSL games and will be key in converting Arsenal’s chances into goals.

The Gunners also showed their fighting spirit in their midweek clash against Barcelona. They drew 1-1 at Camp Nou to become the first side to take points off the Spanish giants in the Women’s Champions League at home since April 2024.

Slegers’ team will feel emboldened by that result but will have to change their tactics against London City.

They have won all seven games against Arsenal so far, scoring an impressive 22 goals and only conceding once. However, given London City’s recent away form, they will be hotly favoured.

They certainly have the quality to take all three points, but they must finally convert their dominance into a comfortable home win.

The Arsenal youngster was introduced from the bench in Friday’s 1-0 friendly loss to Portugal at Ashton Gate. The 16-year-10-month-13-day-old player is over three months younger than Jude Bellingham was when he played his first game for the Under-21s.

Dowman replaced former Arsenal academy player Amario Cozier-Duberry in the 61st minute. He came on alongside debutant Trey Nyoni as England tried to shift the momentum of a challenging game.

An early strike from Afonso Moreira gave Portugal the lead in the 28th minute. An ineffective England team failed to respond. However, the replacements gave Lee Carsley’s team some late momentum.

Despite the hosts’ attempts to level the score, they failed to break down the Portuguese defence. The result means England have lost for the second game running. However, Dowman had much to be pleased with personally.

Dowman has added to his growing collection of records.

He became the youngest player to play in the Champions League, the youngest goalscorer in the history of the Premier League and the youngest to win the Premier League title.

Breaking Bellingham’s England Under-21 record is another significant step. It shows how quickly Dowman has progressed through the international age groups.

He has already made a big impression at Arsenal with Mikel Arteta’s love of giving younger players a chance, but Dowman will have some stiff competition for first team minutes.

Another positive is his progression on an international scale. He will improve both physically and tactically playing against older players and gain experience at a higher level.

England will host France in their next friendly on Monday, 16th November. Dowman will be hoping to feature after his instant impact on the record books.

Despite the disappointing result against Portugal, it was a landmark evening for the Arsenal players.

Dowman is already building a legacy at club level, but now he can add to his list of records by becoming an England Under-21 record holder.

At just 16, he has plenty of time to improve and show consistent performances to get more opportunities with the senior Arsenal squad.

#2058. Martin Ødegaard sends clear message to Arsenal amid Bayern Munich transfer rumours

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Martin Ødegaard has spoken out about the speculation surrounding his future. He has stated he would like to stay at Arsenal for the future.

The captain has also admitted that talks about a new deal have not yet begun. Ødegaard is currently under contract until the summer of 2028. This leaves Arsenal with an important decision to make over the coming months.

Bayern Munich are being linked with an interest in the midfielder according to reports from Germany. The Bundesliga giants are said to be keeping their eyes on the player’s situation.

Speaking while on international duty with Norway, Ødegaard was quick to dismiss the speculation. He made it clear he is settled in north London and sees his future being at the Emirates Stadium.

There is no suggestion that the 27-year-old is seeking a move. Although comments do highlight a contract issue that Arsenal will be keen to resolve in the short term.

The Norwegian’s laid-back attitude should be encouraging for supporters.

He has made it clear that he is happy at the club and wants to stay here for the time being. This means that there is no need to panic.

However, Arsenal will have to get him to sign on the dotted line. Leaving his captain in the last year of his contract with no progress would cause an unnecessary distraction.

Since his permanent move from Real Madrid in 2021, Ødegaard has become a key player in Mikel Arteta’s plans. He has grown into a team leader and is one of the most influential players in the dressing room.

His importance has been shown by his inclusion in all 10 of Arsenal’s Premier League games so far this season. He has scored three goals.

This is a big improvement on last season, where he was hampered by injuries and failed to make much of an impact in front of goal.

It wouldn’t be a shock to see Bayern Munich show interest in Ødegaard, but don’t take this as a sign he is close to a move.

There is little reason for Arsenal to consider losing their captain. He brings so much more to the team than just his technical ability and has been relied upon by Arteta to lead by example.

The midfielder was also pivotal in the 1-0 win over Hull City on 7 November, scoring the winner in the 72nd minute to give the league leaders three crucial points.

Arsenal have put themselves in a good position in the title race. Keeping their key players happy will be important in the second half of the campaign.

The Gunners will be focused on their game against Newcastle United on 21st November.

Arsenal fans have no real reason to panic at the moment, with the captain wanting to stay at the club and his comments suggesting he is happy.

However, it would be a good idea for the club to try and ensure his long-term future at the club. Ødegaard is still an important part of Arteta’s strategy, and ensuring he stays at the club would be a smart move.

#2056. ‘Looking back…’ – Alexander Isak speaks out over penalty controversy in defeat to Arsenal

Alexander Isak has spoken out about the controversial penalty incident in which he was involved during Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal a fortnight ago.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz netted the only goal of the match, the Reds’ number 9 had his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber inside the box, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR deemed it to have been a foul.

The transgression was unmistakably clear on replays, and the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents panel has since acknowledged that a spot kick should’ve been awarded.

Speaking to reporters whilst on international duty with Sweden, Isak was asked if he felt that he should’ve had a penalty.

He replied (Aftonbladet, via Liverpool Echo): “Yeah, looking back I suppose it does look that way, but when you’re in the moment, you don’t always perceive exactly what’s happening.

“I could feel myself being pulled a bit, but not to the extent that it appears later on. I was focused on scoring. It’s hard to try to score and then fall down at the same time. I was so locked in on the goal that I didn’t really register it.”

On whether he should’ve gone to ground to try and sway the referee, Isak said: “I don’t think there’s any need to embellish or go down on purpose. Sure, if I’d had a better read on the situation, I might have made sure the referee noticed it, that’s about all you can do, but I don’t believe you need to dive or exaggerate in situations like this.

“Perhaps it shouldn’t even matter that much, given that we have VAR and systems in place to make the decisive calls in these kinds of moments.”

Isak is absolutely right in saying that a penalty should’ve been awarded, and that he shouldn’t have to act unnaturally to convince the referee to give the decision in his team’s favour.

Andoni Iraola remarked after the game that a spot kick probably would’ve been given if the Liverpool striker had gone to ground, but the onus isn’t on players to sway the officials – it’s on the latter to get these big calls right, especially with recourse to VAR.

It feels as though the debate about officiating in the Premier League will continue indefinitely, with no discernible sign of an improvement in standards from Pro Ref figurehead Howard Webb.

It’s to Isak’s great credit that he’s given such a calm and measured verdict on the penalty incident when he and his team were so blatantly wronged. He’d have had every right to complain profusely about what happened; we’d suspect that many other players would’ve done so if they were in that situation.

He certainly hasn’t let it bother him in terms of his contributions on the pitch, with the 27-year-old scoring in Liverpool’s subsequent games against Fenerbahce and Crystal Palace to take his tally for the season to eight goals in 14 matches across all competitions.

That is, in fact, the best response to the injustice which was done against him Anfield two weeks ago.

Lewis Hall outclassed Lamine Yamal in Madrid.

England by a huge distance the better team and going 3-0 up in less than an hour, it should have been more.

Spain massively got away with one as moments of madness from Jarell Quansah, Elliot Anderson and Anthony Gordon, threatened to destroy what had been a supreme team performance.

With England so much on top, their individual errors in a 12 minute second half spell directly led to the two undeserved Spanish goals and Thomas Tuchel’s team having to play the final 30 or so minutes a man down.

Somebody who didn’t put a foot wrong was Lewis Hall.

We have to now pay tribute and give our thanks to those in the media who have now suddenly ‘discovered’ the brilliant 22-year-old.

I wonder what lifelong Newcastle United fan Lewis Hall has been up to these last few years…?

Lamine Yamal had played in 32 competitive matches for Spain, where they had won 27 of them, drawing five and losing none.

Then the winger ran into Lewis Hall, again.

Lamine Yamal losing in his 33rd competitive appearance for Spain, his first ever.

The only surprise about this Lamine Yamal v Lewis Hall contest was that anybody should be surprised.

It was only in March this year that the pair were up against each other when Newcastle United hosted Barcelona at St James’ Park, Lewis Hall up against Lamine Yamal.

Lamine Yamal scored a fortunate late equaliser from the penalty spot, however, there was no doubt about who won this duel of top class winger and elite lifelong Newcastle United fan.

Barcelona star man Lamine Yamal wasn’t able to dribble past Lewis Hall even once in the 90+ minutes. Whilst the United defender was superb going forward, creating five chances, the most created by any player on the pitch.

On top of all of that, the appalling referee failed to book Lamine Yamal for a cynical foul on Lewis Hall, after yet again the NUFC player got the better of him. A yellow card which would have been Yamal’s third in the competition and seen him suspended for the second leg.

Last night in Madrid was very reminiscent of St James’ Park in March, the only joy Lamine Yamal got was when he was marked by somebody else out wide, or when he came inside to get away from Lewis Hall. Plus of course those two awful errors from Quansah and Gordon that led to the Spanish goals.

It was also amusing to see once again last night, what happens when things go against a young prima donna such as Lamine Yamal. His diving was so impressive and his petulance was a joy to see as he reacted to Hall and England’s dominance with fouls of his own as things weren’t going his and Spain’s way.

#2053. For Newcastle United these are now the steps that matter

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

There are Newcastle United seasons that announce themselves with the flourish of a fanfare, and there are seasons that arrive more quietly, almost tentatively, as if testing the ground beneath their feet.

This one, for Newcastle United, belongs firmly to the latter category.

Ten Premier League matches into the 2026-27 campaign, the Magpies sit in twelfth place with twelve points. Three victories, three draws, four defeats.

The numbers are neither catastrophic nor comforting. They are, instead, the arithmetic of transition.

After years of ascent under Eddie Howe—punctuated by European nights and the rare, precious taste of silverware—the club has entered a deliberate, if painful, period of reconstruction. Key figures have departed. Younger, less seasoned players have arrived. And into this unsettled landscape has stepped Matthias Jaissle, a thoughtful German coach still learning the particular cadences of the Premier League. Let’s pray he is precocious!

The style he favors—“vertical football”—is direct, urgent, and ambitious. Yet in these early weeks it has often looked unfinished, like a promising manuscript that still requires careful editing. Attacks break down before they fully form. The midfield sometimes lacks the necessary ballast. Set-pieces, once a source of both goals and defensive security, have lost their edge. Chance creation has been modest. The underlying numbers suggest a side that is still searching for its rhythm.

I would argue that the back half of last season under Eddie Howe, and with the “superstars” who moved on to their perceived “bigger” clubs, the performances were no better. I flew 3,500 miles to attend the Bournemouth match – at great expense may I add – to witness the worst Newcastle United performance in my near 50 years of following the club. The rot started last season (and I would venture to say in the summer of 2025).

None of this should surprise those who have followed the club’s longer story. Newcastle has always been a place where ambition and constraint exist in uneasy conversation. The Saudi ownership brought resources and expectation, but the financial rules of the modern game impose their own discipline, that I wish would be challenged in court as anti-competitive.

The past 2026 summer window reflected that reality: significant investment, yes, but also the departure of established leaders (good riddance to the rats!) and the calculated gamble on potential rather than proven readiness.

Still, there are concrete steps available this season—practical, unglamorous steps that can steady the ship without pretending the rebuild is already complete.

Matthias Jaissle must first allow himself the freedom of pragmatism. The purest version of his vertical approach has, at times, left the team exposed and the attack under-supplied. A measured adjustment—greater control in build-up when the high press is broken, tighter rest defence, a clearer structure for the attacking midfielder—need not abandon the philosophy. It would simply make it sustainable. Restoring set-piece competence would be another quiet victory. These are matters of coaching detail, not revolution.

The Newcastle United squad itself still holds untapped value. Joelinton’s physical presence and ball-winning capacity remain essential once fully available, but we have a young gem in Sean Steur who, whilst not as physically imposing as Big Joe, is poised, creative, and doesn’t mind sticking a foot in. Dan Burn’s leadership and aerial strength can stabilise both ends of the pitch. The younger summer arrivals require patience but also clear pathways and honest assessment. A stable selection, built around those who are ready rather than those who might be ready later, would help establish the consistency that has been missing.

Then there is January. The winter window is rarely the stage for transformative spending at a club managing financial ratios carefully. Yet it can be the stage for precise, intelligent reinforcement. The most glaring absence is a natural number ten—a player capable of receiving between the lines, linking midfield to attack, and providing the creative spark that current options have not consistently delivered.

One name that has already circulated is Bilal El Khannouss of Stuttgart. The Morocco international attacking midfielder was reportedly considered during the summer and is claimed to be available for a fee in the region of no more than£40 million, a figure that may prove more attainable than many alternatives. His profile—technical, progressive, comfortable in the half-spaces—aligns with what Jaissle appears to seek. Other options will be examined, of course. The market rarely offers perfect solutions in January. But the principle is clear: a ready-made creator who can accelerate the adaptation of the system would be more valuable than another project requiring time the club may not fully possess this season. Contract situations must also be addressed with clarity. Players entering the final year of their deals create both risk and opportunity. Selling at the right moment, rather than losing assets for nothing, can fund the necessary additions while maintaining squad balance.

None of this guarantees a return by Newcastle United to the higher reaches of the table overnight. That would be unrealistic. What it can provide is direction—a sense that the transition is being managed with purpose rather than simply endured. A top-half finish, or even a secure mid-table campaign accompanied by improved underlying performance, would represent genuine progress under the circumstances.

Football clubs, like the cities they represent, are defined as much by how they navigate difficulty as by how they celebrate success. Newcastle has known both extremes in recent years. The current chapter is quieter, more complicated, and less cinematic than the ones that preceded it. Yet it is no less consequential.

The work of improvement rarely arrives with trumpets. It arrives in adjustments of shape, in the careful acquisition of the right player at the right moment, and in the daily insistence that potential must eventually become performance. For Newcastle United this season, those are the steps that matter. The rest will follow, or it will not. But the path, at least, can be chosen with intention.

#2051. Scott Parker’s ‘training session reveal’ shows clean break with Nuno’s strategy | West Ham United

With key players absent on international duty, these mid-international break training sessions are challenging for coaching staff who are keen to improve the team but of course don’t get to drill the whole squad.

West Ham United, though, with their reduced circumstances this season, have fewer players away than in the ‘old days’ of the Premier League thanks to player departures and others – like skipper Jarrod Bowen – simply being overlooked by their national coaches.

#2050. Scott Parker Reunion Could Be Key to West Ham Defensive Deal

No sooner had Scott Parker been appointed as West Ham’s ‘promotion specialist’ manager than stories surfaced linking him with the recruitment of former players.

Reports linking West Ham with C J Egan-Riley are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, with the former Burnley defender continuing to attract attention following his rapid development this season.

Egan-Riley enjoyed a breakthrough campaign previously under Scott Parker, establishing himself as one of the Championship’s standout young defenders and helping Burnley secure promotion back to the Premier League.

A move to the London Stadium would carry several attractions. Not only does Parker know the player well from their time together at Burnley, but Egan-Riley would also qualify as a home-grown player, an increasingly valuable asset for West Ham who are looking to balance squad registration requirements.

Parker has consistently praised the defender in the past, and stated he was a key player for him in the Championship. He was instrumental in the defender’s development, giving him a prominent role in Burnley’s promotion-winning side. His composure on the ball, ability to play across the back line and potential for further improvement make him the type of profile West Ham are expected to target.

Defensive stalwart for Scott Parker’s West Ham?

The central defender chose Marseille ahead of West Ham in 2025, who secured his signature on a free transfer after the expiry of his Burnley contract, meaning any transfer fee received would represent a substantial profit on their investment.

Having been a bit part player at the French club in his first season, following a squad overhaul in the summer he is now a regular starter and the data shows he has maintained a 93% pass completion in Ligue 1. The 23 year old ranks as one of the leagues most accurate passers in his position.

There is also reason to believe Marseille would be willing sellers. The French giants have made no secret of the fact that they will need to generate funds through player departures during the January transfer window due to ongoing financial issues. West Ham have enjoyed a productive relationship with Marseille over the years, with deals for Dimitri Payet, Emerson and Nayef Aguerd demonstrating that negotiations between the two clubs are far from uncommon.

The structure of any potential deal, be it an initial loan or a straight transfer, is yet to emerge. Either way, if the Hammers can persuade the defender to play a part in their quest for promotion they would be adding a young, home-grown centre-back who appears far from reaching his full potential.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2049. ‘Willingness from all parties’ – Transfer insider ‘optimistic’ over Liverpool contract renewal

One transfer insider has claimed that Liverpool may be ‘quite optimistic’ over agreeing a new contract for a high-profile first-team player.

Since turning 18 in August, Rio Ngumoha has been eligible for a longer-term deal at Anfield and, with it, a significant wage increase; and Fabrizio Romano indicated in October that ‘active conversations’ are ongoing over a prospective extension for the teenage winger.

Lewis Steele hinted that a new deal for the youngster should be a matter of when and not if, and the player himself said in an interview last week that it was a ‘no-brainer’ to swap Chelsea’s academy for the Reds two years ago.

Speaking on the Transfer Insider podcast for Football Insider, Pete O’Rourke also talked up the probability of Ngumoha signing a new contract at Liverpool, with both parties likely to want that conclusion.

The journalist said: “Ngumoha is happy at Liverpool. Liverpool are very happy with him. He came out in an interview earlier this week saying that his move to Liverpool was a no-brainer, that he was happy that he made that decision to leave Chelsea for Liverpool.

“I would imagine there’s a willingness from all parties to get a new contract done, so I’d imagine Liverpool are quite optimistic that they will get this sorted.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

With Ngumoha having been given his big break into senior football at Liverpool and featuring regularly under Andoni Iraola this season, we’re also confident that he’ll pen a new contract at Anfield in the coming months.

He’s currently on £35,000 per week from the deal that he agreed in September 2025, which puts him among the Reds’ lower first-team earners (Capology), but we’d suspect that’d increase to six figures with the next extension that he signs in L4.

Since breaking into the senior setup just over a year ago, the winger has never looked back, taking to the elite level with a swagger and a confidence which is rare for players as young as him and even winning a handful of England caps.

Liverpool have other major contract situations to resolve over the next few months – Alisson Becker and Virgil van Dijk are nearing the end of their deals, and speculation continues to abound over Alexis Mac Allister – but keeping Ngumoha at the club for the long-term would be, to use his phrasing, a no-brainer.

It might take another little while yet for full confirmation to arrive, but we share O’Rourke’s optimism that the teenage forward will pen a new long-term contract at Anfield in the near future.

#2048. “Cashing in” on Castellanos claim ignores one major stumbling block | West Ham News

Ever since the closing days of the summer transfer window there have been claims that West Ham will be cashing in on Taty Castellanos in the winter: The Argentine has been a huge disappointment in the 15 games of West Ham’s championship season, with just a solitary goal to show for his efforts.

At times he’s resembled more of a moody, disinterested bystander and seems pretty much the most likely player in the eleven to be yellow carded each time he plays.

A solitary goal is plain unacceptable for the frontman who cost £27 million: Claims that he’ll be sold in the winter abound.

Sadly, Everton’s late interest in the summer window, reportedly around £40 million, appears to have evaporated as Taty’s form has waned. Understandably.

Far from happy: One goal in fifteen means Castellanos has been a huge let down in the second tier. Its also means those big money suitors have now evaporated

The newest suggestions from EFL specialist site the72.co.uk suggest Castellanos could be heading back home – however there’s a catch:

“River Plate reportedly view the 28-year-old as a priority target in their striker search, although the finances involved in the deal could prove to be a major hurdle. However, cashing in could give WHUFC the chance to sign a true talisman to aid their promotion bid. “

“Cashing in”? I think not: That’s the elephant in the room here. River Plate have already disclosed that they’ll look at some kind of loan or shared purchase option – as they’re short of funds – which of course will cut no ice with West Ham who will want to replace Taty with a striker more suited to scoring the Championship goals they require.

Merely shipping Taty out on loan without a permanent sale will serve no useful purpose and could actually weaken Scott Parker’s squad. The Hammers have enough loaned – out unwanted stars as it is: Another one added to the list won’t help a rebuild. The only possible route could involve a swap for goal keeper Santiago Beltran – which would still leave the Hammers short of a goal scorer and needing to offload Hermansen or Areola in the winter.

And how often to these player swaps ever come off? Exactly.

#2046. International quality Newcastle United defence that will provide platform for success

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The Newcastle United defence has been the subject of much focus this season.

Not a lot of the debate on it has been positive.

So has the criticism that’s come the way of the Newcastle United defence been fair?

In the ten Premier League matches so far, this has been the story of the Newcastle United defence.

Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Liverpool 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Spurs 0 Newcastle 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Bournemouth 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Leeds 4 Newcastle 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Hull 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Coventry 4 Newcastle 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 0 Aston Villa 1 Amar Dedić, Fabian Schar, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Crystal Palace 0 Newcastle 2 Amar Dedić, Fabian Schar, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 0 Everton 1 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Fulham 1 Newcastle 1

What I think should be acknowledged first of all, is that we have lacked a settled Newcastle United defence. Injuries playing havoc.

Secondly, there has been undeniable improvement. The Newcastle United defence leaked 13 goals in the opening six Premier League matches, only three goals conceded in the last four. In the last six and half hours (including added time) of Premier League action, United conceding just those three goals, an average of around a goal conceded each 130 minutes following the defeat at Coventry.

This is not to say the United defence were almost faultless, more a case of they are improving.

When you look at those three goals that were conceded most recently in the Premier League, it gives added information. The Villa goal came when a cross from the right eluded Lewis Miley, a midfielder playing out of position at right-back. The Everton one was pure and simply a poor error from Lukas Hornicek who allowed a low standard cross to squirm under. Then the one at Fulham came via deflections off both Thiaw (in the build up) and Burn (to turn it beyond Hornicek.

Yes the opposition had other chances in these games but not loads.

Reality is as well that if Newcastle United had managed at the other end to score a couple of goals in each of these last four matches then it would have been 12 points out of 12 in the last quartet of Premier League games.

That is very different to the opening half dozen EPL matches, where Newcastle United scored six goals in the four games against Liverpool, Coventry, Leeds and Bournemouth but that only brought two points from a possible 12. The Newcastle United defending a lot better against Tottenham and Hull for the two victories early on, with only a single goal conceded in more than three hours of football against that pair.

Now though I think things could go to another level again with this Newcastle United defence, if a bit of fair luck starts going our way on the injury and fitness front.

An international level Newcastle United defence.

Lewis Hall is brilliant, for England and Newcastle United. Surely no doubters amongst you on that one.

Dan Burn has been a huge miss in the opening seven Premier League matches this season. No coincidence only two goals conceded in the three EPL matches he has started on his return after a length injury spell. He has now backed that up with how he has performed for England in recent days.

We saw last season how good Malick Thiaw can be and I think the Fulham match definitely suggested than alongside Dan Burn we could at last have the best available partnership in place finally, of the current NUFC squad. Thiaw has started the last three Germany matches under Jurgen Klopp and they have only conceded one goal.

Tino Livramento was back in the Premier League matchday squad at Fulham and these couple of weeks should have brought him along further. For me there is no doubt about Tino’s quality, the problem has been getting him injury free and back to full fitness on a consistent basis.

Lukas Hornicek has had an up and down start with Newcastle United but taking everything into consideration, I think he has shown plenty to suggest he can do well, especially if he has a regular back four in front of him who have the capacity to give him decent protection week in week out.

Having the three England internationals and our German international making up a Newcastle United back four has huge potential to build the kind of solid platform NUFC need this season.

If Tino Livramento continues to have injury and fitness issues, I believe Amar Dedić is capable of doing a very good job in his absence. I think the Bosnian defender has done okay overall so far, having made the huge step up to the Premier League and walking into what was a chaotic NUFC situation.

If we can have the Newcastle United defence performing consistently well, that then gives us far more chance of improving things further up the pitch, helping United to have far more control of matches and giving a much more positive platform for midfielders and attacking players to prosper.

#2045. The one key question on which nearly all West Ham fans are in agreement

It is not often that West Ham fans appear unified over anything, after recent seasons of strife, division, disagreement and dispute with the Sullivan and Brady leadership, it feels as if ‘disharmony’ has been the default setting.

Not, it seems, about everything. There is one hot topic on which a huge majority of West Ham fans are in almost total agreement.

According to the NY Times’ fan survey, the biggest consensus was not for the approval of the new manager – although there is a pretty strong 77% majority of fans who responded who give the appointment of Scott Parker the thumbs up.

The biggest single factor on which most West Ham supporters agree is the choice of goalkeeper. According to the survey:

“Of the fans surveyed, an overwhelming 85.4 per cent believe Alphonse Areola should reclaim the No 1 jersey from Mads Hermansen.

Likeable yes, dependable no: 85% of West Ham fans want Hermansen out of the team

Interestingly, though, a sizeable 62 per cent of supporters believe the travelling contingent at Ewood Park were not right to boo Hermansen.”

Eighty five percent of fans have had enough of the Dane’s inept performances in between the sticks, with one fan driven to comment that West Ham’s goal would be better defended simply by hanging a green jersey on the cross bar rather than continuing to select the out of form Hermansen.

Of course the fly in the ointment is that Areola has been reported as ‘unfit’ – whether that means third choice Finlay Herrick comes into consideration – who can say- but it’d be a brave selection for Parker to leave his number one on the bench if Areola isn’t ready for the Preston North End fixture next weekend, however much it seems supporters want to see Hermansen out of the team.

Interesting to read through these BBC Sport ‘neutrals’ comments, following on from England defeating Spain.

The hosts going 3-0 down inside an hour as the visitors blew them away.

England goals coming from Kane (pen), Konsa and White, though it could have been five or six up if Thomas Tuchel’s side had turned their superiority into the goals it deserved.

Spain had not lost a competitive game since March 2023, some 44 matches ago.

A daft red card for Elliot Anderson and goals gifted by Quansah and Gordon caught in possession, Spain threatened to keep that unbeaten record going.

However, the final scoreline read Spain 2 England 3 and Tuchel and his players absolutely deserving of the victory against the World Cup winners.

Always interesting to hear the ‘neutral’ perspectives on the England players.

The BBC Sport readers comments from neutrals…

‘Quansah costing Anderson (who got punished for trying to save a teammate) and nearly ruining what turned out to be a memorable night. But overall, brilliant England and that included Quansah.

The player that makes me smile, did a job on Yamal (has an unpleasant side), is Lewis Hall. Something about his determination and composure. Really like him.’

‘Lewis Hall could become something special’

‘Weren’t you predicting an easy win for Spain? 6-0 I think you said.’

And another great performance by Lewis Hall.

‘Agreed, Hall and Trafford both played well; and White deserves a mention too. Scored the winning goal and made an important block near the end.

‘England in cruise control until Quansah did what Quansah does. Again.’

‘Huh?? It was Anderson that was sent off.’

‘Because of Quansah’s lack of concentration.’

‘It was Quansah who got caught in possession, even if it was a foul.

I said beforehand that he is a disaster that has already happened.’

‘Why is everyone calling out Quansah and not Gordon?’

‘Not only him, why did Gordon after a perfect performance try showboating in the middle? He had passes on and declined them to look good. He’s a brilliant player, no need.’

‘Yamal’s reputation is the most closely protected commercial asset in football.’

‘Hopefully one day when five nil down someone will put him in the stand.’

‘Thinks he is the greatest player on the planet. But he isn’t.’

‘He’s been bigged up on the strength of a handful of early performances.

‘Lewis Hall played well against him – so much belief.’

‘What a game against the world champions and arguably the best England performance in many years.

‘…and well done Tuchel. The team is evolving tactically.’

‘They look like a club side now – he’s built something.’

‘Hall was excellent, Trafford grew magnificently into the game.’

‘Well done england. Best performance I have seen in a very long time.’

‘Are Spain turning into Argentina, rolling around trying to con the officials every tackle.’

‘Wow. What a game. Congratulations to England. Deserved win. The full backs Ben White and Lewis Hall were fantastic.’

‘Who would have thought after 62 minutes that Trafford would be man of the match??’

‘Fantastic performance by England against a whingeing,moaning ,diving Spanish team.Special mention for young Trafford in goal,outstanding.’

#2043. Taking instructions from a schoolboy and showing class at half-pace... William Saliba made impressive injury comeback for Arsenal Under-21s - now he faces fight to take Ezri Konsa's spot, writes ISAAN KHAN

Published: 06:24 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 06:28 EST, 11 November 2026

It was a scene straight out of Will Ferrell's Elf. In the middle of Arsenal's Under-21 team huddle stood William Saliba, all 6ft 4in of him, towering over his teenage team-mates as 17-year-old captain Marli Salmon delivered his pre-match rallying cry.

One of the world's finest defenders was taking instructions from a schoolboy.

For the hundreds of Arsenal supporters who had descended on Boreham Wood's Meadow Park on Sunday, it was an extraordinary sight. Four months after suffering a back injury in France's World Cup semi-final defeat by Spain, Saliba was finally back on a football pitch.

But his carefully managed 45-minute appearance in a 5-2 victory over Aston Villa's Under-21s marked the beginning of another challenge. Saliba must now win back a place in an Arsenal defence which, remarkably, has barely missed him.

That is largely down to Ezri Konsa, the £55million summer signing from Aston Villa who has been so impressive in Saliba's absence that Mikel Arteta faces a genuine selection dilemma.

Saliba and Gabriel have been Arsenal's established central defensive partnership since the opening day of the 2022-23 season. But Konsa, arguably Arsenal's outstanding defender this term, has made a compelling case to keep his place.

William Saliba towered over his teenage team-mates and played 45 minutes on Sunday

His performance in the 1-0 victory at Liverpool, Arsenal's first win at Anfield in 14 years, was particularly impressive. He won every ground duel, made 14 defensive contributions and completed eight clearances, leading the match statistics in all three categories. Liverpool failed to register a shot on target.

It was precisely the sort of performance that has given Arteta something to think about. And the Arsenal manager is understood to have challenged Konsa to fight for his place rather than simply make way for the returning Frenchman.

There is another solution. Konsa can operate at right back, a position he has occupied for both Villa and England, including during the summer's World Cup. That would allow Arteta to restore the Saliba-Gabriel partnership without sacrificing a player who has become such an important part of Arsenal's defence. For now, however, there will be no rush.

Saliba's injury history explains why Arsenal have been so careful. In 2022-23, another back problem kept him out for 97 days and contributed significantly to the collapse of a title challenge that had seen the club spend 248 days at the top of the Premier League.

Arsenal have since finished runners-up again and finally claimed the title last summer, but the lessons of that earlier setback have not been forgotten.

Leading back specialists were consulted over Saliba's latest injury before the club settled on a conservative rehabilitation programme, deliberately extending his recovery rather than risking another setback.

He returned to full first-team training last Tuesday, ahead of Arsenal's 2-1 victory over Slavia Prague, but Sunday's appearance represented his first competitive action since July. His absence from France's squad during the international break should allow Arsenal to continue building his fitness without interruption.

And there was plenty to suggest that the long wait has done little to diminish his quality.

The Frenchman is building up his fitness after four months on the sidelines

Saliba faces a tough test to try and break up the partnership formed by Gabriel and Ezri Konsa

Playing comfortably within himself, Saliba repeatedly strolled past opponents before threading passes through the Villa midfield. At times he ventured so far forward after set-pieces that supporters began joking about whether he fancied himself as a centre-forward.

Even at half-pace, the gulf between a world-class defender and academy football was obvious.

Yet it was Saliba's interaction with his young team-mates that provided some of the afternoon's most revealing moments.

Throughout the first half he could be heard directing Salmon, shouting 'man on,' 'high, high' and 'well done, Marli' as he guided his teenage defensive partner through the game.

When Arsenal scored their opening goal, Salmon initially stayed back rather than joining the celebrations. Saliba promptly ordered him forward to enjoy the moment.

Marli Salmon, pictured laying a wreath for Remembrance Day, was the one barking out instructions and seeing Saliba (left) among the youngsters was an extraordinary sight

It was a small gesture but typical of the interest Saliba has taken in Arsenal's younger players during his rehabilitation.

He is understood to have spent time asking about their families and offering advice about life in professional football.

One particular message has been the importance of looking after their parents if they are fortunate enough to make a successful career in the game. The affection is clearly mutual.

Children clamoured for autographs as Saliba arrived and departed, while Arsenal had prepared for the unusual attention surrounding an Under 21 fixture.

Large QR codes directing spectators to the team line-up had been displayed around the ground and a member of the first-team security staff accompanied Saliba between the dressing room and the pitch.

His afternoon was meticulously choreographed. At half-time, his work completed, he disappeared into the changing rooms before leaving through a side exit.

Saliba made his comeback for Arsenal's Under 21 side after a long injury absence

The 45 minutes will have provided reassurance to Arteta and Arsenal's medical staff, as well as a memorable afternoon for the teenagers who shared the pitch with him. For Saliba, though, the real work is only beginning.

Few would have imagined when he suffered his injury in July that he might return to find his place under threat. Konsa's performances have changed that calculation.

Arsenal have their defensive cornerstone back. Now Arteta must decide what to do with him.

#2038. Fabrizio Romano warns of ‘increasingly complicated’ situation which is brewing at Liverpool

Fabrizio Romano has warned that the future of one player at Liverpool is ‘becoming increasingly complicated’.

Long-serving goalkeeper Alisson Becker is into the final year of his contract at Anfield, but he recently expressed his desire to extend his stay at the club, and his agent has reportedly entered ‘preliminary talks’ with LFC chiefs over a prospective new deal.

With the Brazilian’s status as number 1 firmly intact, it leaves Giorgi Mamardashvili playing a backup role and having to be patient for opportunities, a situation that he might feel a compulsion to change in the foreseeable future.

In a video on his eponymous YouTube channel, Romano outlined that the Georgian mightn’t be prepared to wait for his chance for much longer if Alisson were to extend his contract.

The transfer reporter said: “Liverpool are no longer masters of Alisson’s destiny, let’s put it that way. Last summer they were able to say, ‘Stay with us, we’ll extend for another year, we’ll activate the option.’ Now that option has expired, so Alisson can decide his future.

“There is certainly a possibility that Alisson will remain at Liverpool. However, the situation involving him and Giorgi Mamardashvili is becoming increasingly complicated.

“This is because Mamardashvili is not a player who wants to remain a backup goalkeeper indefinitely. He is playing second fiddle while waiting for the door to open for a starting spot at Liverpool and at some point, a decision will have to be made.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Romano’s information echoes that of James Pearce a few weeks ago when the latter indicated that, if Alisson were to stay put, his understudy wouldn’t accept a third season of playing backup to the Brazil veteran.

The role of a second-choice goalkeeper is a peculiar one. They’re only one twist of fate away from getting what could be their big break, but they could be left waiting months (if not years) for that sliding doors moment.

Mamardashvili hasn’t yet managed to seriously challenge our number 1 for a place in the starting XI, but the Georgian has produced some strong performances in the Carabao Cup this season, including one world-class save against Tottenham in the third round in September.

Even his status as Alisson’s immediate deputy could come under threat from next year once Lucca Brughmans arrives from Genk, although that chain of command would be contingent on the Brazilian’s future at Liverpool.

We can see it from Mamardashvili’s perspective – he’s 26 now and won’t want to fritter away too much of his career warming the bench – but it’s essential for the Reds to have a solid succession plan in place for life after their long-serving number 1, whose world-class presence will be extremely difficult to replace.

#2036. Soccer hooligans descend on Australia: Wild footage shows horde of fans smashing cars and damaging property

Published: 03:01 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 07:38 EST, 11 November 2026

Shocking footage of soccer fans after a match has reignited complaints about public safety, following previous warnings repeated violence was putting families at risk.

Perth Glory supporters have demanded action over a confrontation near HBF Park, with video posted on social media showing a group of young people as they crowded around a parked white vehicle and aggressively rocked it from side to side.

Other footage filmed from across the road shows young people confronting fans in the street, with the group spread across the footpath and roadway outside nearby businesses.

Images shared alongside the complaints show fighting on previous occasions, as well as damaged fences and other property. Supporters allege the material documents a recurring problem involving the same group and have demanded bans and stronger security measures.

The footage prompted calls for bans and renewed criticism of matchday security, with supporters alleging genuine fans face strict enforcement over minor issues while more serious behaviour goes unchecked.

'The same group of troublemakers causing chaos and mobbing random people', one fan posted on social media platform X.

Young people crowd around a parked white car and aggressively rock it near HBF Park in footage that has sparked anger among Perth Glory supporters

Supporters allege genuine fans are being left feeling unsafe at Perth Glory matches

Tagging Perth Glory, they added: 'It's time you do something about it. People have had enough.'

The supporter also called for individuals to be banned and, in a subsequent post, alleged nearby property had been damaged.

WA Police, Perth Glory and A-Leagues have all been contacted for comment.

Perth-based football podcast and digital channel The Far Post Perth shared the original post, adding its own demand for intervention.

'Not a good look at all and something needs to be done about the problem at this point, genuine supporters are being impacted,' the account wrote.

One commenter alleged the group had been moving through the venue during the match while being followed by security and police.

'This is the mob that was walking back and forth all game with security/police following,' they wrote.

'We don't need this at HBF Park. It makes many people feel unsafe when these wannabe thugs just shove their way through.'

Another video shows young people confronting fans on the street outside nearby businesses

Photographs of damaged fences and other property have fuelled calls for stronger action

The person who posted the footage claimed that 'after the game the police and security were nowhere to be seen'.

They also shared a separate video from February, alleging it showed an earlier confrontation involving the same group.

The February post had complained about people attending matches in The Bay supporter area and allegedly fighting with other young spectators.

The complaints follow a strongly worded statement issued last year by supporter groups The Bay Perth and Shed End Perth, which demanded sanctions after a separate incident outside Gate 2 during the second half of a match at HBF Park.

The groups said they were aware of footage circulating online and distanced themselves from those involved, alleging physical confrontations had become a recurring problem.

'We want to make it absolutely clear that those involved are not fans and do not represent our supporter groups, our values, or the wider football community,' their joint statement read.

'These individuals consistently attend matches with the sole intention of causing problems rather than supporting the team, and their behaviour is completely unacceptable.'

The statement alleged confrontations had occurred in active supporter areas and the Eastern family stand, extending the groups' concerns beyond the stadium's most vocal sections.

Images shared alongside the complaints show fighting on previous occasions

'In almost every single game, they have caused physical confrontations in both the Active areas, and in some cases the Eastern family stand too, and it is deeply frustrating that this behaviour continues without meaningful consequences,' the groups said.

They alleged the behaviour was damaging the experience of supporters who attended matches to follow Perth Glory.

The groups also accused matchday security provider NPB Security of failing to respond adequately to incidents.

Their criticism included allegations that a rotating contingent of inexperienced security staff was being deployed and that personnel were unable or unwilling to intervene when serious problems arose.

'The lack of accountability from NPB Security is unacceptable and has undermined the safety of the matchday environment,' the statement read.

'Warnings and passive responses are clearly not working.'

The groups called for bans and other sanctions, warning that further incidents could affect spectators and people working at the ground.

'Without firm action, including bans and real consequences, these so-called 'fans' will continue to put genuine supporters, families, and staff at risk.'

They urged the club and stadium authorities to identify those responsible and impose firm sanctions.

Their earlier warning has been followed by fresh complaints about how security rules are enforced at Perth Glory matches.

'Meanwhile security go OTT about bottled water in the shed or actual fans taking t-shirts off,' one supporter wrote in response to the latest footage.

Another commenter similarly complained that removing a shirt in the supporter bay could result in ejection, while alleging people involved in violence escaped consequences.

The Far Post Perth also challenged a response that dismissed the latest incident as 'kids being kids'.

'Kids being kids is vandalising other people's property? Interesting,' the account replied, referring to the allegations of property damage.

However, one person responding to the original footage questioned whether those shown in the street were Perth Glory supporters.

'In the second video, the person filming is standing where the stadium is. These idiots look like they are walking from the other side of the road,' the commenter wrote.

'Are we sure they are even Glory fans? Or just troublemakers.'

The person who uploaded the footage insisted they were, although the posts do not establish that the same individuals were involved in each of the incidents raised by commenters.

The Bay Perth and Shed End Perth had made their position on violence explicit in their earlier appeal for action.

'Violence, fighting, and antisocial behaviour have no place in football,' they said.

'HBF Park, The Shed, The Bay and all areas of the ground should be a safe and welcoming environment for all supporters, families, players, and staff.'

#2034. How Liverpool feel about January recall for Ifeanyi Ndukwe amid Premier League loan enquiries

Liverpool are reportedly keen for Ifeanyi Ndukwe to continue his development on loan with Levante in Spain, despite the player now being eligible for a UK work permit.

The 18-year-old was a revelation for the Reds in pre-season but, at the time, he didn’t meet the criteria to play competitively in England and was subsequently dispatched to the LaLiga outfit for this season.

He’s continued to perform impressively for Los Azulgranas, and there were reports last month of his agents arranging to discuss the possibility of a January recall to Anfield.

According to Graeme Bailey for TEAMtalk, Liverpool are convinced that Ndukwe could break into their first-team setup next year and view him as ‘hugely important’ for their long-term plans.

Although he could theoretically be recalled in January, the Reds’ preference is for him to remain with Levante for the rest of his season and proceed with his development there.

That hasn’t stopped some Premier League clubs from enquiring about his availability for a loan move for the second half of the campaign to give him a first taste of English top-flight football.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Having had to wait until October for his first start for Levante, Ndukwe was then included from the first whistle in all six of their LaLiga games since the extended international break earlier in the autumn (Transfermarkt).

Luis Castro demonstrably has faith in the Austrian teenager, whose performances on loan have earned praise from the Spanish media, although the occasional error has served as a reminder that he’s still developing and will have off-days as part of that.

While Premier League exposure would be a quite informative barometer of the youngster’s readiness for the Liverpool first team, we’d be in favour of him continuing with Levante if he’s enjoying regular game-time there.

At the moment Ndukwe is featuring regularly in one of Europe’s foremost domestic leagues, and doing so with a club where media attention and scrutiny is comparatively sparse, thus keeping him away from the harshest of exposure.

He must be doing plenty right to have English top-flight clubs asking about taking him on loan in the winter. If that’s the case, then the current plan seems to be working, and we see no reason to deviate from that any time soon.

#2031. Championship data highlights exactly what West Ham’s midfield is still missing

A fascinating piece of Championship analysis from Loft Insights on X may provide an uncomfortable reminder of where West Ham’s midfield falls short.

The graphic plots central midfielders based on two key metrics: line-breaking passes per 90 minutes and ball-winning actions per 90 minutes. Put simply, it measures which players are able to progress the ball through opposition lines while also contributing defensively.

The most interesting takeaway for me was not necessarily which players stand out, but where West Ham’s own midfield profiles sit on the chart.

The Championship’s elite midfielders increasingly occupy the top-right quadrant, combining progression and defensive intensity. That is why the chart identifies Norwich City’s Kenny McLean as one of the Championship’s most complete midfielders, posting outstanding line-breaking numbers while maintaining strong defensive output, despite only featuring for ten games out of fifteen due to an ankle injury.

Meanwhile, Portsmouth’s Ebou Adams is highlighted as a “defensive monster”, producing exceptional ball-winning statistics while still offering significant progression. Sheffield United’s Kalvin Phillips (yes the same player that flopped on loan at West Ham!), Queens Park Rangers’ Jonathan Varane and Norwich’s Jacob Wright also occupy impressive positions, demonstrating the ability to impact both sides of the game.

Mohamadou Kanté is viewed as a dynamic ball-carrying midfielder with strong physical attributes, but his game is built more around energy and transition play than elite progression metrics. Arne Engels offers technical quality and creativity, yet is generally more comfortable operating higher up the pitch than acting as a defensive controller.

The data is only based on players who have played an average of 540 mins so one omission is Tomas Souček, whose strengths have always been obvious. The Czech international on paper would arguably be the Championships most effective midfield goalscorer (3 in 7 appearances so far) and I’d expect him to feature highly for aerial presence. However, if plotted on a graph measuring line-breaking passes and ball-winning volume, he would likely owe more to his physicality and attacking threat than his ability to dictate possession through midfield.

That perhaps explains why West Ham can sometimes appear disconnected between defence and attack.

Too often there is a reliance on direct balls into attacking areas rather than building through the centre of the pitch. Equally, when possession is lost, the midfield does not always possess the combination of mobility and defensive output needed to regain control quickly.

West Ham arguably have midfielders who can create and win duels. What they appear to lack is a genuine “two-way” midfielder capable of consistently ranking highly in both categories.

That was precisely what Declan Rice offered during his time at the club. His ability to recover possession and immediately progress the ball remains incredibly difficult to replace.

The reality is Rice was never truly replaced, although finding a like-for-like successor was always going to be a near-impossible task

Former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse’s position on the chart is also interesting. A casualty of Nuno’s reign, he ranks among the highest players for line-breaking passes but has one of the lowest ball-winning outputs. Ward-Prowse excels at progressing possession but offers relatively little defensive contribution compared to the league’s most complete midfielders.

Above all the data serves as a reminder that Koppen’s recruitment and Parker’s existing choices for midfield should focus less on individual statistics and more on complete profiles.

Because the numbers suggest that is where Championship matches are increasingly won.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

I think there is nothing wrong with the Midfield. There is just a problem with the short pass mentality. The day of playing short passes across midfield are over in English football. You need decent long passes with good trapping and decent positive movement. How many of West Ham’s passes are square ball or back passes ? Far to many. Particularly back passes are all to often caught on to giving away needless goals. Walker-Peters is a really good example. Having moved forward beating someone, he then passes back in midfield, or worst still carries the ball backwards towards midfield or defence. Play positively, avoid back passes, learn to pass well and trap well and you have a very good midfield. Orford, Kante and other young players are far better at doing this, than the older players.

#2029. ‘They had different ideas’ – Rafa Benitez opens up about ‘difficult’ Hicks and Gillett era at LFC

Rafael Benitez has opened up about the ‘difficult’ time that he had at Liverpool during the damaging ownership era of Tom Hicks and George Gillett.

The American businessmen bought the Merseyside club in 2007 amid grandiose promises about a new stadium in Stanley Park (‘a spade in the ground within 60 days’, and all that), but they quickly became hugely unpopular figures among the fan base.

As the duo ultimately fell out with one another amid a period of civil war at the club, debts mounted to the extent that LFC was on the brink of administration in 2010 before they were ousted by a takeover from New England Sports Ventures (now Fenway Sports Group).

In an interview with The Athletic, Benitez was asked if he ever thought back to what could’ve been for Liverpool had it not been for the damaging ownership of Hicks and Gillett, throughout which time the Spaniard kept the club challenging for major silverware.

The former Reds boss reflected: “Yes, 100%. When Hicks and Gillett came, they changed the approach. All the things you did for the benefit of the club, they had different ideas. I realised, and the fans realised later, that something was wrong. They didn’t have experience of football.

“I remember speaking to Gillett once in London after we played Tottenham. He said: ‘We will give you money and then next season you’ll get us into the play-offs.’ I had to tell him there were no play-offs.

“They thought maybe: ‘Rafa is a threat.’ That period was difficult, but all I ever wanted was the best for the club.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Benitez’s final season at Liverpool in 2009/10 was a major disappointment, with the Reds expected to challenge for the title but slumping to a seventh-place finish, and there was a prevailing sentiment that the time was right for a change in the dugout.

However, as the extent of the damage done by Hicks and Gillett became clear in subsequent months and years, the latter part of the Spaniard’s managerial reign has come to be viewed in a much kinder light.

He was left with an impossible job of trying to achieve success on the pitch while all sorts of strife was going on in the background, slowly eating away at the club until John Henry rode to the rescue in October 2010.

Benitez’s time at Liverpool may have ended on a low ebb, but he remains a greatly appreciated figure among the fans for delivering Champions League glory in Istanbul and getting the Reds back to being a competitive force domestically and on the continent, even if the Premier League eluded him.

Had it not been for the incompetence of those at ownership level, who knows just how much more the Spaniard could’ve achieved at Anfield in the late 2000s and possibly into the 2010s?

#2027. West Ham Winger Faces Another Fitness Test As Parker Waits

West Ham United are facing something of a dilemma over Manor Solomon, with Israel reportedly considering bringing the winger back into the team for Tuesday’s Nations League clash against Austria. The 26-year-old has been struggling with back pain during the international break, although Israel manager Ran Ben-Shimon has suggested that he is feeling better after returning to training.

According to Sport5, Solomon could now be in contention for the Austria fixture. That follows comments from Ben-Shimon suggesting the player had trained and was feeling better, although his fitness would need to be reassessed.

For West Ham manager Scott Parker, however, the situation presents an interesting dilemma. We desperately need the old Manor Solomon back, but I wonder whether another international appearance is really what the player needs right now.

Manor Solomon representing Israel during a difficult international break. The West Ham winger has been carrying a back injury since October

Look, I’m caught between a rock and a hard place on this one.

There is part of me that hopes Solomon gets a game, so he can get back to form. Because there’s no doubt about it, West Ham have a far bigger chance of getting promoted this season if Manor Solomon is back to the sort of form he was in when he played for Leeds in the Championship.

Clearly Scott Parker has faith in him because he has seen how destructive he can be in that division. Getting that player back would be a significant boost for the Hammers, particularly with the Championship promotion race starting to get serious.

But, and it’s a big but, we have had complaints of back injury during the October internationals, and we’ve already had it during this international break.

As I reported earlier in October, a West Ham source confirmed that Solomon was in considerable pain after an exhausting international schedule. More recently, we reported on his latest back problem, which restricted his training with Israel.

There is also part of me that wonders whether we would not have been better served, and the player himself, actually resting up, getting some medical treatment, or even being given ten days off completely to recuperate and joining back up with the squad for the last few days of training before the Preston game.

As things stand, there’s nothing in his recent form that suggests he could start and should start against Preston. And without him being on the training pitch during this international break to impress Scott Parker, he’s not going to be able to catch the manager’s eye.

Edvin Austbø has certainly given Parker something to think about on the left wing. Indeed, Austbø’s recent performances have highlighted the competition for Solomon’s place, and I suspect the Norwegian is currently ahead of him in the pecking order.

But I don’t want to write off Solomon. We know what he’s capable of producing in this division, and West Ham will need every bit of attacking quality available if we’re serious about getting back into the Premier League.

Hopefully, Israel will make the sensible decision and only involve him against Austria if he is genuinely fit enough to play. We cannot afford another international break to leave us with a player who returns to east London carrying another injury.
