#1973. There's still a place in the modern game for managers like Kevin Blackwell, says former Hearts and Rotherham United striker

Kevin Blackwell has been in charge of Crawley Town on an interim basis since the end of October following the sacking on Colin Kazim-Richards after a terrible start to the season for the Reds.

The 67-year-old has a vast amount of managerial experience including jobs at Leeds United and Sheffield United and, despite an embarrassing exit in the FA Cup to seventh tier Wimborne Town, has had a good start to his Reds stint with four points in two league games.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

And Washington, in his latest exclusive EFL column for BestBettingBonuses.co.uk, is happy to see Blackwell involved.

“I think it's great to see genuine football people like Kevin still involved in the game,” he said. “Football feels very modern and young at the minute, and sometimes it seems like coaches are inventing new vocabulary every other week to describe things we've been doing for decades!

“The reality is that so much of what we're seeing tactically has been done before in some way, shape or form. Of course the game evolves and you have to adapt with it, but the fundamental aim of football hasn't changed.”

And he added that experience can be seen as detrimental sometimes when it comes to older managers. He said: “So much of management is still about understanding people, building relationships and helping players through difficult situations. I think we're sometimes too quick to dismiss experienced managers or label them as dinosaurs because they might talk about defending deep rather than playing in a low block.

" Ultimately, they're describing the same thing, and just because someone doesn't use the latest terminology doesn't mean they don't understand the game.”

But Washington said experience is what Reds need right now. “In Crawley's situation, I think having someone who's experienced difficult periods before and isn't afraid to be demanding could be exactly what the players need,” he said.

"That doesn't necessarily mean being abrasive for the sake of it, but sometimes players need clarity, honesty and someone who's prepared to make difficult decisions.”

But should Blackwell be considered for the job permanently? Washington said: “I think that should come down to the impact he has on the players and the results he gets, rather than any preconceived ideas about his style or personality.

"There's absolutely still a place in the modern game for managers like Kevin, and I think it would be a shame if we lost sight of that.”

#1972. Chelsea injury update: Joao Pedro, Emi Martinez, Josh Acheampong latest news and return dates

Your weekly briefing on Chelsea, featuring team news and expert analysis from Dom Smith

Chelsea could welcome back two key players from injury as Premier League action resumes this weekend at home to Leeds.

The Blues went into the final international break of the year on the back of a crushing defeat to Sunderland as Xabi Alonso’s side had no response to Enzo Le Fee’s penalty - which was awarded a few minutes after Cole Palmer had controversially seen a claim for a spot-kick of his own turned down following a VAR review.

As such, Chelsea have dropped down to fifth in the table, though there is likely to be some positive news regarding Emi Martinez and Joao Pedro - who both missed the loss to Sunderland - in the next few days.

With that in mind, here is the latest Chelsea injury news and return dates…

Josh Acheampong was a surprise absentee from the Chelsea matchday squad at the Stadium of Light, particularly as the youngster had started all five matches prior.

It quickly became clear, via Alonso, that the defender was dealing with a minor issue. The good news is Acheampong is not expected to be sidelined for an extended period, though he was forced to withdraw from England U21 duty.

“He is recovering from a minor thing. He missed the fitness to be ready for today but we are expecting that he will be back after the international break,” Alonso said of Acheampong before the defeat to Sunderland. “It’s a pity because he was in a good moment.”

After the game, the Chelsea manager added:“There are situations. Yesterday Josh felt something and he was not fit to play. So we are shorter in options and we need to go through this time.

“Even when we win, or when we lose, we miss some players that we have injured and for sure we are waiting to have them back because they are important.

“Now we need to use the time to recover them, but with the players we have, we have to get ready for the next one.”

Potential return date: Saturday November 21, vs Leeds (H)

Martinez has now missed Chelsea's last four games across all competitions after undergoing surgery for a broken jaw sustained upon a collision with Jarrad Branthwaite in the win over Everton last month.

The Argentina international was expected to be sidelined for around six weeks, but has made a swift recovery. He returned to training ahead of the Sunderland game and was in contention for a start, but it was ultimately decided that he would not be risked.

#1971. The nine major strategic blunders Ineos have made at Man United that prove they cannot be trusted to choose Michael Carrick's replacement

Published: 21:00 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 13:20 EST, 11 November 2026

Michael Carrick looks set to pay for Manchester United’s miserable start to the season with his job this week – but removing him won't fix the club's deep-seated problems.

Carrick took more points than any other Premier League manager between his arrival as Ruben Amorim's interim replacement in January and the end of last season.

He was rewarded with the job on a permanent basis but the Carrick era has quickly unravelled and United entered the November international break 18th in the Premier League, out of the Carabao Cup at the first hurdle and middling at best in the Champions League.

Carrick's dismissal is the latest shameful episode for Ineos, who took control of football decisions in February 2024 when Sir Jim Ratcliffe came on board as a minority owner.

Daily Mail Sport understands CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox still retain Ratcliffe's backing despite being the subject of fan chants calling for their dismissal at recent matches.

Berrada and Wilcox have failed time and time again and yet seem to escape accountability. Here are nine Ineos mistakes that have dragged Manchester United into the unlikeliest of relegation battles – and raise the question of whether they should be trusted to get the next managerial appointment right.

Michael Carrick's dismissal is the latest shameful episode for Ineos, who took control of football decisions in February 2024 when Sir Jim Ratcliffe came on board as a minority owner

Carrick looks set to pay for Manchester United’s miserable start to the season with his job this week – but removing him won't fix the club's deep-seated problems

Erik ten Hag looked to be on thin ice from the moment Ineos walked through the doors at Carrington.

One of his first conversations with the new hierarchy saw the Dutchman offer to put together a plan to overhaul United’s failing data department. The offer was rejected.

‘I offered my knowledge and abilities to Ineos to help them to construct, but they were of the opinion that they already knew everything,’ Ten Hag told The Athletic recently. ‘They were convinced of, say, the philosophy, the strategy, the work methods. But they came from petrochemicals, from Formula 1, from cycling. Top football demands something totally different.’

That summer, Ineos were caught on the hop by the groundswell of support to keep Ten Hag after United beat rivals City in the FA Cup final, when all indications were they had been ready to sack him. Ineos were put in an awkward spot. That said, they still openly flirted with other managers just days after United’s Wembley victory.

Future England boss Thomas Tuchel met with Ratcliffe in Monaco before he dropped out of the race. Gareth Southgate, Mauricio Pochettino, Thomas Frank and Roberto De Zerbi were considered as Ten Hag remained in limbo, all while United navigated the situation without a sporting director or a CEO.

In the end, with tail between legs, an Ineos delegation flew to Ibiza to interrupt Ten Hag’s holiday and agreed to extend his contract by a year, make changes to his coaching staff, as well as make promises for the upcoming transfer market.

Ineos were caught on the hop and kept on Erik ten Hag (right) after United beat rivals City in the FA Cup final, when all indications were they had been ready to sack him

‘They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned,’ Ten Hag explained. ‘We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep.’

According to Ten Hag, Ineos went back on their word having said they would not sell Scott McTominay, who joined Napoli that summer for £27.5million, and the manager was sacked 116 days after his deal was extended with another £200m splurged in the transfer window.

By the time Ten Hag was finally dismissed, with a compensation package of £10.4m for him and his coaching staff, Ineos had wasted close to a quarter of a billion through indecision.

Ratcliffe relentlessly pursued Dan Ashworth as he sought an elite sporting director to lead the new sporting structure. He believed the Englishman to be ‘clearly one of the top sporting directors in the world’ and ‘a very capable person’.

Ashworth spent five months on gardening leave after United eventually agreed a near-£3m compensation package with Newcastle United to get him, only to be gone after five months in the North West.

Ratcliffe would go on to blame Ashworth for the decision to stick with Ten Hag and there was a sense that Ashworth was not on board with the move to bring Ruben Amorim in. It all culminated in his shock exit after a 3-2 home defeat by Nottingham Forest in which he was escorted through the press room at Old Trafford with his head bowed en route to a meeting where he was sacked.

Ashworth was paraded as a move that showed Ineos could deliver on their ‘best in class’ mantra, only for them to ditch him embarrassingly quickly.

Dan Ashworth (second right) was paraded as a move that showed Ineos could deliver on their ‘best in class’ mantra, only to embarrassingly ditch him less than six months later

Sir Dave Brailsford, one of Ratcliffe’s most trusted lieutenants, was also an unmitigated disaster. He started off as a crucial figure behind the scenes and his ‘marginal gains’ mantra became a key focus for everyone as he led the renovation of the Carrington training base.

Brailsford drove the appointments of Omar Berrada and Dan Ashworth, and was one of the key men behind ‘Mission 21’, United's bid to win a 21st Premier League title, and ‘Mission 1’, to win a first Women’s Super League title. Both fell under the ‘Project 150’ umbrella he was particularly proud of, to win titles in the club’s 150th anniversary in 2028.

Sixteen months after coming in, Brailsford was removed from day-to-day operations and earlier this year he fully separated from the club by coming off the board.

Brailsford ran football operations at a time of mass redundancies, fans being alienated by ownership, a failing team that produced its worst Premier League finish of 15th, and millions wasted in the transfer market on players that quickly depreciated in value.

Ruthless job cuts, something key Ineos figures have long insisted were essential for the health of the football club, totally destroyed morale and have, according to some remaining staff, completely changed the club for the worse.

In July 2024, staff were told of the need to cut 250 jobs, as company credit cards were cancelled, and staff were asked to contribute towards expenses. In February 2025, Ineos announced a further 150-200 jobs would need to be cut all while austerity measures – the scrapping of free lunches among them – escalated.

All of this against the backdrop of the senior executives continuing to be paid handsomely for gross levels of under-performance.

Having arrived as a technical director working under Ashworth, Wilcox soon found himself thrust into the biggest executive job in the Premier League, as director of football at United.

Omar Berrada (right) is a close friend and supporter of Jason Wilcox (left) and trusts him implicitly, as does Ratcliffe, who believes he has the ‘best eyes’ at the club

He pitched up at United having navigated close to nine months in the same role at Championship side Southampton. Prior to that his expertise had been across at Manchester City in youth development.

Berrada is a close friend and supporter of Wilcox and trusts him implicitly, as does Ratcliffe, who believes he has the ‘best eyes’ at the club. Wilcox was one of the driving forces behind the appointment of Amorim and it was he who would go on to clash with the Portuguese at the end, leading to his eventual sacking.

Wilcox is very hands-on, routinely seen close to training sessions, and has travelled with the team on numerous occasions.

‘When I listen to Jason speak, I get what he’s saying,’ Ratcliffe told The Times in March 2025. ‘He’s a warm character, he’s got a sense of humour, he knows what he’s talking about.’

Wilcox has been accused of interfering too much while not establishing the game model Ineos long promised to implement, regardless of who the head coach is. The director of football was called out in a post-match interview by Lisandro Martinez this season and Wilcox has inexplicably remained in the shadows while players and Carrick face up to the club’s failings.

A patchy recruitment record, all while preparing to search for a third permanent manager in less than 12 months, Wilcox has had next to no positive impact on United’s first team since assuming Ashworth’s job.

Hurting from the way they totally miscalculated and mishandled the Ten Hag situation, Berrada and Wilcox pushed to convince Amorim to abandon Sporting Lisbon mid-season – something he did not want to do – and bring his philosophy to Old Trafford.

It was explained that his 3-4-2-1 system would take a long time to embed onto a squad that had been playing 4-2-3-1 but United's decision-makers were undeterred and forked out £11m to get Amorim and his staff in.

It was explained that Ruben Amorim's 3-4-2-1 system would take a long time to embed but United chiefs were undeterred and forked out £11m to get Amorim and his staff in

A further £250m was spent on the squad the next summer but Amorim's standing took another pounding following a League Cup giantkilling at Grimsby Town

Hiring Amorim in isolation wasn’t an error. He represented a bright young manager that had a clear philosophy – something Ineos haven’t shown in two and a half years – but he had been overlooked by West Ham and Liverpool.

One well-placed source told Daily Mail Sport that Liverpool compiled a dossier on all the reasons Amorim would not be able to succeed at Anfield, largely down to how many players would need to be recruited to make his vision a successful reality.

Amorim was ‘rewarded’ with just two arrivals in January 2025 in the shape of Patrick Dorgu and Ayden Heaven, while the following summer saw a clash of ideas in terms of transfer targets. Senne Lammens arrived despite Amorim seeking a veteran goalkeeper to replace the hapless Andre Onana.

Amorim guided United to their lowest Premier League finish and lost the Europa League final in Bilbao to Ange Postecoglou’s Tottenham Hotspur. A further £250m was spent on the squad with the attack overhauled but his standing took another pounding following a League Cup giantkilling at Grimsby Town.

Relations between Amorim and Wilcox deteriorated severely and they clashed in a meeting on the eve of the trip to Leeds United, which would prove his final game. Amorim unleashed a fierce rant which intimated that figures such as Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell were overstepping the mark with their input and that they needed to allow him to be the ‘manager’ of the club.

Having come under pressure to change formation and the style of play, Amorim was sacked the morning after drawing at Leeds.

Rather than actually devise a plan to deliver Amorim’s vision, Ineos instead tried to get clever and turned to Harry Marra, a renowned track and field coach, to come in as a consultant.

He was given the remit of assessing individual player running mechanics, acceleration and deceleration. Mason Mount was one of those who Marra identified and he attempted to adjust the 36-cap England midfielder’s running gait.

Ratcliffe imparted advice on stretching techniques he had learned from running the London Marathon to figures in the Carrington physio room

Add from the episode in which Ratcliffe imparted advice on stretching techniques he had learned from running the London Marathon to figures in the Carrington physio room, you got the picture of an ownership that didn’t seem to understand that top-level football isn’t track, field, or cycling.

Performance on the pitch only got worse after this, not better.

8. Prioritising new stadium over a new left back

Speaking to reporters in Dublin this summer shortly after being given the United job full-time, Carrick used the word ‘push’ almost a dozen times when referencing what the club still had to do in the transfer market.

But Ineos, again believing they are the smartest people in the room, ignored those pleas and stuck to their plan to ‘fix’ one part of the team per summer. It was the attack in 2025, and in 2026 it would be the midfield, with the defence to come next year.

So, despite knowing full well that expecting another injury-free campaign from Luke Shaw was an enormous gamble, they did it anyway and made no defensive reinforcements. It hasn’t taken long for that move to backfire spectacularly.

Instead, the decision was made to purchase land to the tune of £60m so they can plough on with plans for a swanky new 100,000-seat 'Wembley of the North' stadium that many fans believe will never be built.

Rather than fixing the team's defence, United chiefs spent £60m on a slither of land to progress with their plans for a 100,000-seat 'Wembley of the North'

The way Carrick has been treated in this whole saga has been cruel and a sign of why managers should think twice about taking a job under Ineos

An emergency meeting after a 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last month looked set to be the end for Carrick until Berrada, Wilcox, Ratcliffe and the Glazers surprised the football world and simply did nothing. Everyone just continued with business as usual with no backing for the beleaguered Carrick.

Defeat at Chelsea, coupled with two frantic displays to come from 2-0 down against both Roma and Aston Villa followed. Then came the revelation on Monday that Berrada and Wilcox had settled on a recommendation to the board that they should sack Carrick. But instead of being sanctioned immediately, Carrick spent seven hours at Carrington on Tuesday to take training and watch an Under 17s match.

We are told yet again that Carrick's future will finally be decided on Wednesday at a meeting in Monaco, but in the meantime he must carry on until he gets wind he has been officially sacked.

The way Carrick has been treated in this whole saga has been cruel and a sign of just why managers should – and will – think twice about taking a job under Ineos.

However, the captain’s personal achievement was overshadowed by a dismal performance and result that left Scotland with a record of seven points from a possible 18 and a third place finish in Nations League Group B1.

Switzerland were gifted a first-half opener when Lewis Ferguson turned a harmless cross into his own net before Scotland allowed the roof to cave in by conceding twice in the opening six minutes of the second half.

Strikes from Winsley Boteli and Alvyn Sanches put the hosts 3-0 up before Zeki Amdouni added a fourth in the final minute to increase scrutiny on Pocognoli after a less than impressive start to his tenure.

"We talk about it at half-time to say keep going and by 50 minutes we're 3-0 down. That cannot happen in international football.

"We were playing against a good team but we were in the game in the first half. We have to do it for 90 minutes. Then you're 3-0 down at a tough place. A really tough night for us."

Pocognoli has yet to convince the Tartan Army that he is the right appointment after succeeding Steve Clarke, who resigned after seven years in charge following Scotland's World Cup exit.

Asked if it will take time for the 39-year-old Belgian's methods to bear fruit, Robertson warned: "I don't think you've got time in international football. You have to do it.

"Are those supporters who have travelled everywhere going to give us time? No. Are the people inside Hampden going to give us time? No. Are the people outside Hampden that are going to be critical, and rightly so, going to give us time? No. We've not got time. The players don't have time. We have to step up.

"We now have a long break until March which is not a good thing. It's going to be a tough one to swallow."

#1968. Mile Oak have afternoon to forget at Hailsham

Oak had the best of the early exchanges and were assisted by an early visit to the sin bin for Toby Brett but failed to provide any serious threat to the Stringers goalkeeper.

With Harry Robins suspended it was hoped new signing Sam Geard would provide some creativity but he was forced off through injury before a quarter of the game had passed.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The only threat to the Oak defence was the height of the Hailsham players and just before half-time they came unstuck when a long throw was launched into the box which enabled Michael Lloyd to force the ball in.

The second half saw little improvement in what was becoming a bad tempered game with players swarming around young referee Elliott Brown as a number of fouls were committed by both sides.

Oak did manage to manufacture one chance when Liam Smart headed in but was ruled offside. As the half wore on the Stringers looked the most likely to score as Mile Oak faded away like the autumn leaves.

A disappointed Sam Cornish said: “Unfortunately, it was a really frustrating afternoon. For a neutral it must have been a terrible watch on a lovely 3G surface – neither side looked like they wanted to get the ball down and play.

"We started with a different shape, which was impacted early due to the loss of Geardy, and we never really got any momentum from there on.

"The effort and work-rate was still there from our lads, but the game as a whole lacked any real quality throughout. Having said that, we also didn’t get anything go our way all afternoon & scored a perfectly good goal that was chalked off.

"It’s important we don’t dwell on the what ifs dust ourselves off and go again. Its points dropped, another defeat on the road and we can’t hide from the fact that ultimately our away form is not good enough and is something we must look to rectify quickly.”

Spirited Yapton were generally second-best, but had their moments, especially in the first half.

They trailed in the third minute when a Bosham corner to the far post was neatly headed home. Then Yapton's best efforts were shots from Aaron Tague and Josh Dean that were respectively well saved and scrambled off the line.

Early in the second period Brandon Terry equalised with a superb cross-shot but from that point Bosham took over with some impressive approach work and wrapped it up with goals in the 70th and 85th minutes.

#1967. Tottenham injury update: Mathys Tel, James Maddison, Mykhailo Mudryk latest news and return dates

Your weekly briefing on Tottenham, featuring team news and expert analysis from Sam Tabuteau

Tottenham return to Premier League action on Saturday, but those fitness concerns heading into the international break remain ahead of a visit from Ipswich.

Defeat to Leeds last time out not only halted Spurs’ momentum after three straight wins and a draw, but it was a costly one for Mathys Tel as he left Elland Road wearing a protective boot and needing the aid of crutches.

There has since been an update on the French youngster, and not a positive one at that. Furthermore, James Maddison’s fitness has been called into question after twice failing to be called upon from the bench this month.

However, there is better news on the likes of Savio, Lucas Bergvall and, potentially, Xavi Simons.

Here is all the latest Tottenham injury news and return dates.

Mathys Tel could be out for a significant period after suffering a “bad injury” during the defeat at Leeds, which left him on crutches after the game.

The forward was on the receiving end of a heavy challenge from Leeds defender Jayden Bogle, who landed with his studs up on the Frenchman’s left Achillies but escaped even a booking for the foul despite a VAR review.

Despite initially trying to play on, Tel eventually signalled to come off and was replaced by Dominic Solanke. The young striker was later seen leaving Elland Road on crutches and with a protective boot on as he made his way to Spurs’ team bus.

As confirmed by French Football Federation (FFF), Tel did not link up with the France U21s as a result of the injury, meaning he missed the loss to Italy and will sit out Tuesday's showdown with England.

A statement reads: “Having suffered an injury with his club Tottenham, Mathys Tel is forced to withdraw from the France Under-21 team training camp which began this Monday at the CNF Clairefontaine.”

It still remains to be seen how long Tel will be sidelined for, with a further update likely to follow during the De Zerbi addresses the media in the pre-Ipswich press conference later this week.

Fitness concerns remain regarding James Maddison after failing to come off the bench in Tottenham’s last two games.

Maddison has not played since picking up an issue during the win at Chelsea last month, and De Zerbi opted to turn to teenager Lucas Williams-Barnett instead of the experienced midfielder with Spurs chasing a goal at Elland Road.

“James, I thought [about bringing him on] in the last substitution before Luca Williams-Barnett, but I saw [Mohammed] Kudus was very tired,” De Zerbi explained.

“And James didn’t [train] until Thursday. On Thursday he worked half [and] part of the training yesterday.

“And in the last 15 minutes maybe could be a good solution, but I decided to make that change because Luca in the winger position, is better than Maddison.”

Potential return date: Saturday November 21, vs Ipswich (H)

There was slight hope that Savio would return for the trip Leeds, which would have been ahead of schedule.

This was after Savio was spotted training with his team-mates ahead of the game, having seemingly recovered from the muscular injury picked up against Manchester United last month.

However, the Brazilian was again absent heading into the international break.

The good news, though, is he could now be available against Ipswich, thus bolstering De Zerbi’s attacking options even further.

Potential return date: Saturday November 21, vs Ipswich (H)

Tosin Adarabioyo has been sidelined with a calf injury since making his first start of the season last month, in a win over Coventry, but was back in contention heading into the international break.

Tosin was not involved in the squad at Leeds, having only days earlier returned to first-team training.

De Zerbi said on Friday: “Tosin is available, yesterday he came inside with the group.”

Potential return date: Saturday November 21, vs Ipswich (H)

Lucas Bergvall will be hoping to return from injury after the international break, after missing the last four games for Spurs with a knock.

The initial prognosis was a two-week absence, but now Bergvall will have a fortnight get back up to speed after being left out of Sweden’s latest squad.

Potential return date: Saturday November 21, vs Ipswich (H)

The reason for Martin Dubravka’s absence from the Tottenham squad against Leeds is down to a minor knee injury which prevented him from being named in the Slovakia squad for their Nations League double-header.

Spurs’ back-up goalkeeper is not expected to be sidelined for too long, so a return on the bench against Ipswich is likely.

Potential return date: Saturday November 21, vs Ipswich (H)

Signed on loan from Chelsea in the summer, Mudryk played just one game before picking up an ankle injury in training back in September.

De Zerbi stated the timeframe for the “stupid” injury was six to eight weeks, with it originally hoped that the Ukrainian could be involved by late October. That was then updated to after the Novemver international break.

Potential return date: Saturday November 21, vs Ipswich (H)

New reports suggest that Xavi Simons will enter the final phase of his recovery this month and return to first-team training, having only ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) back in April.

Simons suffered the injury against Wolves and was predicted to return early in 2027.

The Dutchman posted footage of himself training on the grass last month and his early comeback would be a massive boost for De Zerbi.

Frenchman Wilson Odobert is another Spurs player recovering from an ACL injury. The former Burnley man sustained his tear against Newcastle in February.

The typical timeframe for an ACL recovery would have the winger available to Spurs in December, but De Zerbi’s recent comments put that timeline under some doubt.

The Italian stated: “I don't know, because he has not started yet to work with us. I have no idea [when he will return].”

#1966. Thoughts of a lifelong fan: Fingers-crossed for a first home win and a night off for Kabby

I am just about getting over our exit from the FA Cup and the Jersey Mike’s Trophy, watching Exeter City go one up against CTFC (the other one), and in visiting OUR club’s website I was shocked to see we only have just over an hour to go before we play Rotherham away.

We don’t of course, because of international call ups for both sides. The three for Crawley being Dion Pereira, Stephen Duke-McKenna and Nick Michalski. Dion played for 60 minutes for Antigua and Barbuda in a 3-2 home defeat, whilst Nick was in goal for the England U20 side in  a 6-1 win against Czechia and Stephen was scoring a brace for Guyana in a six nil away victory over the Cayman Islands. I hope it’s not too long before he is scoring again for Crawley.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Going back to "us” playing at Rotherham, and with just 40 minutes to kick off, “I follow” will sell you an audio pass to the game if you want to listen, surely this rivals the notice board outside the Broadfield stadium in not showing the club in the best light. In the old days, and I know this makes me sound like everyone’s dad or Uncle Albert, Stan Markham would have the next match on the board at half time while people were still watching the game and we didn't have the internet, but I'm sure we wouldn’t have been advertising something that wasn’t going to take place.

Of course, you can hope for things as much as you want, doesn’t mean that it will happen though, but out of the nine top half v bottom half matches taking place only Colchester United, Port Vale and Fleetwood of the bottom half teams achieved victories. Roch In the weekends League 2 games, which were all on the tele because of the international window, Exeter hung on to beat Cheltenham by one goal to nil in the early game and then, because Joe Comper works for Gillingham and Jay Williams plays for Colchester, I decided to watch that one and of course, was cheering on the Kent side. In all the matches taking place there appears to be an almost top half versus bottom half feel to the fixtures and, because of the predicament we are currently in.

I have to say it would have been really good if the results had gone to form. Jay missed a sitter for the team from Essex in the first half, then got booked for a very robust tackle, which, if it had been committed in a red shirt would probably have got him sent off. Two goals in the second half saw the team I wanted to lose, win their first game in ten so now it was down to the others to perform to my script. Rochdale, Swindon, Bristol Rovers and Oldham all lost, and the Cobblers drew at Salford and Newport drew at Crewe after leading by two goals to nil.

For those of us with short memories, who can’t remember a season where we have started so badly, we need only go back to last year when we sat on exactly the same number of points after the first 12 league games played. We have scored more this season, by three goals, but unfortunately have conceded more as well. In order to ensure we stay in the football league for next season everyone knows we need to start winning games and that is why, as supporters we need to do what it says on the tin and support the lads wearing our colours through all the games left this season. Last year in the next 14 games we won just 10 more points and in the whole season we won just eight games and still managed to survive on the last day of the season.

Hopefully, although Priestley Farquharson appears to be out of contention for a while because of the injury sustained in the defeat at Wimborne, the return of Josh Flint and the arrival of Ben Heneghan will strengthen our defence and Duke-McKenna will add some Guianan magic and start scoring goals for the Red Devils again like he did against Bromley back at the beginning of October and before you know it we’ll be climbing the league ladder to safety.

Can we do it?  Yes, we can, but it must start with us making sure we beat the teams around us rather than those destined at least for the play offs. Don’t get me wrong, I would gladly take three points off the likes of Barnet next Tuesday but the minimum we should expect is for a concerted effort from all those who play for or support this club of ours. Hopefully we will achieve our first home league win here on Saturday against Fleetwood and Kabby Tshimanga will have an off night next week and live up to my friend's opinion that he really isn’t that good.  I wouldn’t bank on that though as back in the day he also said something along the lines of “Paul Fishenden, he’ll never make a centre forward".

I’m going to sign off now, before the men in the white coats arrive, but before I do go for a well-earned Sunday dinner, I would like to say that I am giving up being an optimist for being hopeful. Have a read of the definitions below and see if you should become hopeful too.

Optimism is a generalized, passive expectation or belief that things will turn out well and that positive future outcomes are more likely than negative ones. It looks at the big picture and assumes the future will improve largely on its own, through luck, external circumstances, or the natural order of things.

Hope is an active, goal-directed motivational state. It requires acknowledging current difficulties, pain, or poor odds rather than ignoring them. Hope involves building concrete plans and agency (the personal energy and determination) to act and shape a better outcome, even when the odds are stacked against you. for

Thank you, Christina Cipriani, (Crawley URC) for showing me the light

Here endeth the sermon for this week. Noli Cedere, Never Give Up.

#1964. GdS: Four exclusions, four defeats – Milan’s Pulisic dependance highlighted

There are many ways to outline Christian Pulisic’s importance to AC Milan, but one of them is very simple: wins.

La Gazzetta dello Sport have outlined the fact that when Pulisic starts a match, Milan do not lose. In an inconsistent team like Ruben Amorim’s, the four defeats this season to Benfica, Bournemouth, Bologna and Ferencvaros have two things in common.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The first is the two starters in midfield: four times out of four, the double pivot was Yunus Musah and Ardon Jashari each time. Then, there are the three absentees: Mario Gila, Luka Modric and Pulisic.

Pulisic, Gila and Modric are clearly three of Milan’s key players, and the American arguably more so than the others. He’s eighth in Serie A in points average from starts (2.67 points, five wins in six games).

Pio Esposito, Lulli, Mora (the three who have always won as starters), Zaccagni, Dimarco, Isaksen, and Zielinski rank higher, but there’s a clear difference: the others play for Lazio, Inter, and Roma, the top three in the league.

Captain America came on against Benfica, Bologna, and Ferencvaros, and was an unused substitute against Bournemouth. Compared to Modric, who has been playing consistently since August, and Gila, who has been affected by injury, Pulisic has had his ups and downs.

He scored in Udine, the derby and most recently against Genoa, and it’s no coincidence that the Diavolo won all three games. Simply put: when Christian plays well, Milan follow him. When his level drops, Milan struggle.

It’s tactics, as well as numbers. Pulisic has different characteristics from his team-mates: he’s the only one who attacks the space in behind. Gonçalo Ramos often comes deep and lays it off, Alphadjo Cisse loves having the ball at his feet, and CP disrupts defences in other ways.

Furthermore, he’s considered one of the owners’ key players, who are also American, and he just renewed his contract. If you have to imagine the Milan of the future, just think Pulisic and 10 others.

#1963. Liverpool injury update: Virgil van Dijk, Ryan Gravenberch, Dominik Szoboszlai latest news and return dates

Liverpool are sweating over the fitness of several key players ahead of their clash with Manchester United this weekend.

The Reds will take on United, who welcome Mauricio Pochettino to their dugout at Anfield, but they could be without some of their star names for the fierce rivalry.

They lost three players during the international break to respective injuries, and Andoni Iraola will be hoping that a few days of down time will allow for sufficient recovery.

Van Dijk was forced to withdraw from the Netherlands’ squad to face Greece and Germany in the Nations League last week.

The Reds captain was forced to pull out of the squad for fitness reasons, according to a statement issued by the Oranje FA.

It read: “Virgil van Dijk [and Brian Brobbey] have been dropped from the Dutch national team's upcoming international matches. Both players did not return fit from the past weekend's matches and are therefore unavailable.

#1962. Sheffield Wednesday's Dave Challinor on his summer set-piece education at Brentford

During his time out of work at the start of this season, Challinor visited the training grounds of Celtic, West Bromwich Albion and Brentford amongst others to broaden his horizons.

And the effect of his trip to see the Bees was evident on Saturday as the Owls registered their first win under him courtesy of two goals from set pieces to beat Plymouth Argyle.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Billy Mitchell opened the scoring with a shot which took a massive deflection at a 45th-minute corner. It was the midfielder's first goal since 2021.

Davis Keillor-Dunn then scored his sixth goal in nine matches when the Pilgrims failed to deal with a Callum Slattery free-kick.

Centre-back Di'Shon Bernard completed the scoring with a brilliant individual effort.

"I went to Brentford in the summer for a few days and saw how seriously they take it," said Challinor of set-pieces.

"They have set-pieces as part of every single training session for them, whether it's warm-ups or practise, delivery, finishing will be important. It's something that we are really keen to make sure we do practise and we do work at.

"It's not the most exciting thing in the world is it, practising set-piece delivery, but if you get the reinforcement on a Saturday it makes it a whole lot easier.

"We are really conscious and want to make sure the record we have is a positive one and Saturday helps.

"Keith (Andrews, Brentford's coach) was really helpful in me going up there so I spent a few days with them.

"It's an amazing environment, I learnt so much. There will be things from there that we'd love to incorporate here.

"It's a brilliantly run football club that have the success based on consistency right from the very top."

Wednesday's win, their first in seven matches in all competitions, took them above Tom Cleverley's Plymouth and back into the League One play-off places.

The result, it must be said, was better than the performance, and Challinor was not getting carried away at the end of his first league game as Owls manager, after consecutive cup defeats to begin his reign.

"I think we've got loads to do,” he said. “(At half-time) I was really open with the players and asked them what they thought. Sometimes it takes 10 minutes to earn the right (to play), sometimes it takes 60 minutes, sometimes you never earn the right.

"Plymouth are really good at asking questions of you, and in the first half I don't think we dealt with them questions well enough at times.

"We maybe needed to compete better and win first contacts and drop on second balls and track runners. We probably got away with it a little bit at times.

"But they were really honest about that and said that was the case.

"The second half was much, much better. I thought we dealt with their threats and then we were able to make the game look a little bit more like we'd want it to look like."

#1959. Defender David Bates recalled by Scotland after almost eight-year absence

Published: 13:34 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 13:45 EST, 11 November 2026

David Bates has been rewarded for a strong start to life in Turkey by earning a recall to the Scotland squad almost eight years after his last appearance for the national team.

The 30-year-old centre-back has been added to Sebastien Pocognoli’s group after Luis Binks withdrew ahead of the Nations League matches against North Macedonia on Friday and Switzerland on Monday.

Bates currently plays for Amedspor and has started all 11 matches this season as his club have soared to third in the Turkish Super Lig.

The defender won all four of his caps under Alex McLeish while playing for Hamburg in the 2018/19 campaign. His last appearance for the national team was in a 2-0 win over San Marino in a Euro 2020 qualifier in March 2019, in what also turned out to be McLeish’s last game in charge.

Former Rangers player Bates joined Amedspor in the summer after spending four years in Belgium with Mechelen and then Standard Liege following his Aberdeen exit in 2022.

Brondby captain Binks is the second centre-back to drop out of the squad initially named by Pocognoli last week, after Swansea’s Stephen Welsh sustained an injury and had to be replaced by Los Angeles FC’s Ryan Porteous last weekend.

David Bates playing for Scotland against Albania back in 2018

Sebastian Pocognoli is keen to create a winning culture in the Scotland squad

The head coach is viewing this month’s double-header as crucial to his preparations for the Euro 2028 qualification campaign, which could begin in March if Scotland are not involved in Nations League play-offs.

'I think that these two games are, if we start the qualification in March, the last package of games that we have to use to be ready for the March camp,' Pocognoli said.

'If it’s not the case (that the Euro campaign starts in March), we can play friendly games which can be useful for June, so we have more time to prepare. And maybe, if we are really strong in the next two games, maybe we have play-off games. That’s the ambition.

'These can be useful also for the process of the qualification. But if the qualification starts (in March), we need to be ready. That’s why this camp for me is crucial in terms of demanding to the players, try to impress me and do everything to improve.

'I believe if we want to go to the Euros and be successful, we need to build this qualification feeling by winning games and to build the best winning culture possible.'

#1958. Bexhill United maintain play-off push by beating Seaford Town

With an international break hitting the top-tier domestic game - and on a stunning bright, but cold, late autumn day - the Pirates’ biggest crowd of the season, 226, gathered at the Polegrove to see if Jay Skinner-Swain’s men could kick on with their impressive league campaign to date.

Early signs were encouraging. Ash Latuske, wide on the right, was impressive from the off and on just three minutes he opened the scoring. Jack Shonk brought down a high ball and squared it to Latuske in space in the box and he grabbed the chance to knock it in.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Seaford Town have had a mixed few months of league action but have managed to chalk up some decent results and they now set about trying to claw their way back into the game after the early setback. They opened up a decent chance on 25 minutes but Finn Holter in the Bexhill goal reacted sharply to make a good save.

Minutes later Theo Coombs came close to doubling the Pirates lead, his shot heading wide of the post after he was well set up by Ryan Moir from out on the left.

As the play shifted quickly back down the other end, the pendulum swung again as a Charlie Playford challenge was adjudged by the ref to warrant a penalty. There were few complaints and the Seaford man crashed the ball home to level the score.

It was disappointing for Bexhill, but the team picked themselves up and got back at it straight from the restart. The run-up to half-time saw a period of sustained Pirates pressure.

On 40 minutes Luke Donaldson struck an absolute peach of a volley which Josh Mitchell-Lake in the Seaford goal managed to get just enough of a touch on to divert it over the bar.

That was followed shortly after by an acrobatic volley from defender Dale Penn which just cleared the bar with the Polegrove willing it in as Penn continues his search for that elusive goal.

One all at half-time meant that there was plenty to do.

Coombs has developed a knack in recent weeks of scoring quality goals at crucial moments. Saturday added another to that tally. On 65 minutes he picked up the ball outside the box, surged forwards and drove home a quality finish from distance.

But there was plenty of action and controversy left in this contest and half an hour into the half the ref handed Donaldson a straight red for a first offence that he viewed as dangerous.

Bexhill had played a large chunk of their away game at Seaford with ten men in August and it seemed to inspire them then. Now it had the same effect.

Suddenly Bexhill shirts were everywhere, winning the ball and setting up a wave of attacks. The Pirates made that pressure count with sheer persistence from Shonk creating a chance for himself that he squeezed home from a tight angle.

As Seaford tried to make some use of their one-man advantage they were leaving large gaps at the back for Bexhill to exploit with Moir in particular making hay.

Just after the 90 minutes were up he drove a shot towards goal and, with the keeper out of position, a defender threw himself across the line and handled to stop a certain goal. Off he went with a red card and Shonk blasted in the spot kick.

Deep into injury time Moir came close to nailing the goal he deserved. Breaking clear, shrugging off a challenge and just failed to beat the keeper.

This was a great result for Bexhill in front of a bumper crowd and they aim to keep the momentum going with another home league clash against Midhurst and Easebourne on Saturday.

#1956. Bradford City chief Michael Duff's admission regarding Nick Powell

Namely, the amount of match minutes given to Nick Powell, whose quality has been there for all to see during his game-time so far in 2026-27.

Powell plundered his eighth goal of the campaign after coming off the bench in Tuesday's EFL Trophy cruise against York City at Valley Parade.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It's the 33-year-old's best haul since his Stoke City days in 2020-21-, with two-thirds of the campaign still to go. Duff remains wary.

The City chief said: "Everyone can see that (his quality) but it's a risk every time. Hopefully he gets through this because people are going, ‘what are you playing him in that game for, he's a dead rubber (versus York).’

“He needs to hit certain metrics and certain things during the week and what is the best environment for him to do that in.

“That’s the thing with Nick, he's in a good place at the minute, he's enjoying his football, he's fit.

“So, we need to harness that and keep him fit for as long as possible because when you put him on the pitch, he's going to score goals.”

City, who return to action next Saturday with a Yorkshire derby at home to Doncaster Rovers, have emphatically answered the charge regarding their perceived lack of goals with a 12-goal haul in two big Valley Parade wins over Marine and York City respectively.

Duff continued: "Since the first day we came in, we've definitely created a lot more chances.

“I go back to the Burton game where we've had the keeper made a 'worldie', we've had two off the line and had some good chances in it.

“The Oxford game, we’ve missed three or four gilt-edged chances in that and you look at the run that they’re on.

“The fact that the ball's actually hitting the back of the net, the opposition is irrelevant. We had five big chances in the first half (on Tuesday) and it's 1-0.

“From a coaching point of view, you can't kick the ball in the net for them. But the fact that we're getting opportunities and they're now starting to take their chances, hopefully it sort of just releases the noise.

“All you can do is stay consistent with the way that we work, the way we behave, the way we train.

“No one thinks we don't have quality. Hopefully the confidence starts going, they don't overthink it and then it becomes more natural.”

“We knew Eastbourne would have plenty of the ball, but we defended brilliantly at times and created some very good opportunities ourselves. On another day, we could easily have gone in front, and I think that would have changed the game.

“I was disappointed with the decision when Freddie went through in the second half. From where I was standing, it looked a clear foul, and those are the decisions you need to go your way in tight games like this.

“Matt has been outstanding for us recently, but I thought everyone put in a tremendous shift. The second goal came when we were pushing to get something from the game, which was frustrating.

“The performances are certainly improving, and the lads deserve enormous credit for their attitude and commitment. However, we can't keep talking about playing well and coming away with nothing. Nations League fates will be decided this evening as Germany and the Netherlands face off in a mouth-watering showdown between two European heavyweights.

Both teams are largely in control of their own destiny, though a draw would certainly suit the Dutch more as it would be enough to top Group A2 and secure home advantage in the quarter-final second leg - which will be played in March 2027.

Germany, now managed by former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss Jurgen Klopp, can finish first but must beat the Netherlands and hope Greece fail to do so against a Serbia side that has lost all five matches thus far.

The reverse fixture between Germany and Netherlands finished all square in September as Cody Gakpo denied his former manager (Klopp) victory in his first game in charge of the national team with a 92nd minute equaliser in Amsterdam.

The Dutch have gone on to win three times since, including a 7-0 thumping of Greece on Friday night, but are without a win over Germany since September 2019.

#1946. Prince William asks Aston Villa boss Unai Emery about the team EVERY DAY - as he reveals he's become a bigger supporter since becoming a father to football-mad George

Published: 07:23 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 14:24 EST, 11 November 2026

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery has revealed how passionate Prince William is about his beloved football club and opened up on their relationship.

The Prince of Wales, 44, has been a fan of Villa since his days at Eton when he idolised club legend Paul McGrath - shunning the more conventional Premier League big beasts supported by his schoolmates.

He regularly attends matches at Villa Park and across Europe alongside his son George, and he has been a prominent figure during their success under Emery in recent times.

This included the Prince partying with Villa's squad after last season's Europa League triumph and he watched them against Barcelona in the Champions League at the Nou Camp last week.

And, in a special edition of Country Life magazine, which was guest edited by the 44-year-old, Emery reflected on their relationship and how often they talk about the club.

’During the transfer window, he’s asking about the team every day,' the Villa boss said. 'How is the team? How are you? How are we going to play some players? How are we going to do? He is always so close to us and we appreciate it so, so much.

Unai Emery has revealed how passionate Prince William is about Aston Villa and opened up on their relationship

The Prince pictured alongside his son George at Villa's game against Barcelona last week

A special edition of Country Life, guest edited by the 44-year-old, featured a piece on Emery

’When he’s with us, he’s a fantastic guy. We’ve had lunch together, he’s watched training sessions, we share conversations, everything about football. He shows his humble personality with us - I can’t forget it. For me, it seems unbelievable.

'He’s our boss, but he’s always trying to be at our level, respecting so much everything we are doing here. If he’s sitting with us to have lunch, he asks “Where am I sitting?” Wherever you want! It’s fantastic.

‘We are scoring, he is celebrating, it is fantastic for us. If we can give him good news, good results, good moments in football, we are proud of it.’

In the same article, the Prince of Wales went on to reflect on his love of football and Villa, revealing how he has become increasingly passionate over the years.

He added: 'Football feels like a second family to me, I love the tribal nature of being among others who support the same team. We all experience the highs and lows of following that team together and you get the feeling that you belong somewhere.

'I used to be a defender, usually right back, and I’m hoping to play in a few fathers’ five-a-side matches. Since having children, I’ve become even more fanatical than I thought I would be about the game.

'I wasn’t like this when I was 18 or 20, I kept an eye from a distance. Now, I probably think and talk about Aston Villa every day. I enjoy looking to see what is going on: the stats, the players’ recovery, tactics and matches.'

The Prince is regularly pictured watching his beloved team at Villa Park and across Europe

When asked previously about why he settled on the Midlands club, Prince William shared that it was the thrill of supporting a club without season after season of successes which had brought him to Villa.

'A long time ago at school I got into football big time. I was looking around for clubs. All my friends were either Man United fans or Chelsea fans and I didn’t want to follow the run-of-the-mill teams,' he told the BBC in 2015.

'I wanted to have a team that was more mid-table that could give me more emotional rollercoaster moments.

'Aston Villa’s always had a great history. I have got friends of mine who support Aston Villa and one of the first FA Cup games I went to was Bolton v Aston Villa back in 2000. Sadly, Villa went on to lose to Chelsea (in the final).

'It was fantastic, I sat with all the fans with my red beanie on, and I was with all the Brummie fans and had a great time.

'It was the atmosphere, the camaraderie and I really felt that there was something I could connect with.'

#1944. Who will England face in Nations League quarter-final? Next opponents confirmed after Spain win

England are on course to record their best ever performance in the Nations League, having qualified for the quarter-finals as group winners ahead of world champions Spain.

England player ratings: Surprise Arsenal star scores 8/10 as huge statement issued

Ice warnings in force with motorists urged to take care

How to watch Germany vs Netherlands: TV channel and live stream

Including its inaugural season in 2018/19, the Three Lions have competed in every single Nations League campaign, experiencing some highs and the lowest of lows.

From topping their group and qualifying for the Nations League finals and finishing third to suffering a shock relegation in 2022/23 and then immediate promotion, England have done almost everything except win the competition.

Having started the 2026/27 campaign with a loss to Spain, despite leading 2-1 at one stage, England bounced back in style by beating the Czechs twice and then thumping Croatia 7-0 in a remarkable, record-breaking rout.

Another win over Croatia followed at Wembley to confirm a top-two finish in the group and qualify for the Nations League knockout stage.

England then beat Spain in a one-game shootout in Madrid to win the group and with that, potentially securing, an easier quarter-final tie next March.

The four group winners will face the four runners-up in a two-legged Nations League quarter-final.

The group winners will all be seeded and will have home advantage in their respective second leg ties. Teams from the same group cannot be paired together in the knockout stage, therefore England and Spain - for example - will be kept apart.

As a result of finishing top in Group A3, England’s one confirmed potential Nations League quarter-final opponent so far is Belgium after they were pipped to top spot in Group A1 by France.

England’s remaining possible quarter-final opponents will be revealed over the next couple of nights, but as things currently stand, they could be drawn against either Greece or Denmark.

The draw for the 2026/27 Nations League quarter-final will take place on Friday, November 20 with the ties scheduled to take place in March 2027.

#1942. Wilson’s wondrous finish seals FA Trophy win as Eastbourne Borough close door on Curfews

Tyano Wilson, just 18, had been pitched into the action by manager Steve King on 74 minutes in a last attempt to break the deadlock ahead of a potential penalty shoot-out – and the young man seized his opportunity.

A pass into his feet, just inside the box. A touch, a swerve to the left, and just enough space and sight of goal. A fizzing left-foot shot that found the top corner with Chertsey keeper Luke Roberts clutching at thin air: 2-1 and the Sports had claimed a memorable victory.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

It had been a cracking contest, and the visitors had played a full part. Borough had slightly more of the ball and slightly the better chances, but after claiming a ludicrously early lead, they never put the game to bed – and a fateful red card, late in the first half, had put the home side at a disadvantage for an hour.

What a start for the Sports. After successfully defending two Chertsey corners in the first two minutes, the home side broke with Josh Rees through the right channel and Terrell Egbri blitzed down the touchline. He raced on to the pass, a touch, a delightful looped cross just too high for startled keeper Roberts, and there at the back post was Paul McCallum to head home.

But the Curfews – among the leaders in their own Southern Premier division – had not come south for a charabanc outing, and they responded strongly. Liam Nash saw his 25-yarder spilled for a Borough corner – from which Chertsey raced the length of the pitch and almost equalised.

The high pace was matched by some physical moments, too. Chertsey had copped one early yellow card, but they escaped sanctions for a couple of heavy challenges, a blatant handball and an obvious trip on Liam Nash in the area.

On the other hand, Freddie Carter was fortunate to escape without a card for one pretty blatant challenge on Nathan Minhas 20 minutes, and these marginal moments tend to even out. Chances were being traded like swap cards.

Then, a potentially game-changing moment. After an apparent elbow in Egbri’s face had been unpunished, Borough left-back Nathan Laleye did incur the ultimate sanction four minutes before half-time: a little wrestle with Chertsey danger man Minhas was judged a denial of a scoring opportunity – and Mr Black flourished red.

Arguably Carter – spared his own red card earlier – was in a covering position, but referees do not have multi-angle replays, and the Sports would have to play for almost an hour a man down. King responded at once by replacing Darren McQueen with full-back Elliott Johnson.

Alex Fisher, on a yellow card, escaped a second caution after first fouling Egbri and then kicking the ball away.

After half-time, Chertsey were on the front foot at once. Minhas put one effort too high and a second chance wide, but Borough were feeling anything but comfortable. The minutes were clicking away, painfully slowly for home supporters but a little anxiously for the Curfews – until exactly at the mid-point of the second half, the visitors had their chance.

Harry Phipps, working overtime at the heart of defence, tripped Leo Farruch, who had just spurned a priceless chance. A clear penalty, and Minhas seized the chance to equalise from the spot.

One-all, and as the Curfews pressed their one-man advantage, the Sports were digging deep. Their best chance seemed to be the penalty shoot-out – or could the ten men somehow snatch a winner?

Veteran semi-pros only grit their teeth and and resign themselves. But buoyant 18-year-olds, unleashed off the bench, seize the moment.

And Wilson, in those final 15 minutes, would claim the moment. Into added time, he took possession a yard inside the Chertsey area, shimmied left to open up a sight of goal, and smashed a dream of a shot into the top right corner. Despair for the Curfews, elation for the Sports.

#1941. England: How many games Elliot Anderson will miss after Spain red card

Elliot Anderson is facing a suspension after being sent-off in England’s Nations League win over Spain.

Goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White had the Three Lions cruising to victory at 3-0 on Sunday night, before Anderson’s challenge on Lamine Yamal produced both a red card and a penalty.

Mikel Oyarzabal successfully converted the spot-kick before substitute Nico Williams reduced deficit with 15 minutes plus stoppage time remaining.

Ultimately, England held on for a famous win and topped Group A3 as a result.

England will discover their quarter-final opponents later this week, but they will be without Anderson for the first-leg because of the red card.

UEFA rules stipulate “a player or team official sent off by the referee is automatically suspended for the next match in the competition.

“In the event of a serious offence, the UEFA disciplinary bodies are entitled to augment this punishment, including by extending it to other competitions.”

Due to Anderson being given his marching orders in the Spanish capital for denying an obvious goalscoring opportunity, rather than violent conduct, his punishment will be a one-game ban.

Therefore, the Manchester City midfielder will be available for the second leg in March 2027 - if named in the England squad by Thomas Tuchel.

Tuchel, meanwhile, slammed the decision as a ‘double punishment’ during his post-match press conference, dissecting a classic England performance after becoming the first team to beat Spain in 43 competitive matches.

Tuchel commented: “The red card and the penalty is always a big decision - and I need to understand why it's a double punishment.

"Then it was a long, long 30 minutes - but I don't want to focus on that. There was so, so many positive things about the result after 60 minutes. It was well deserved.”

#1938. Nones makes little piece of Oval history – and Eastbourne United make it three wins in a row

Common have had a poor start to the season, United quite the opposite, sitting in second place at the start of a day on which the latest addition to the ground was unveiled – an electronic scoreboard at the Seaside Road end.

Early on, there seemed to be a somewhat frantic attempt by most in the United team to be the one who registered the first goal on the new board, with Joe Overy looking like he had new batteries installed.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Four times he opened up the Common defence, but Callum Barlow, Ryan Blunt and Overy himself all shot agonisingly wide, and Jorge Nones had one well saved.

With 25 minutes gone, Barlow was hauled down in the box but the referee inexplicably waved play on. The ball was loose, everyone dived on it and Brett Patton’s sidefooted effort won a corner. Cometh the hour, cometh, well the boy - 35 minutes were showing on the new scoreboard as Nones kept a cool head to drive past Matt Crutwell to make it 1-0 to United. He will forever be the first scorer to have his name on the new board.

The second half proceeded with remarkably little incident – there was somehow an inevitability that if Common did too much, United would go and score, so a kind of detente broke out.

Deep into the second half, Alieu Secka had one of those moments that goalies specialise in, terrifying the crowd as a mix-up led to him scrambling to push the ball round for a corner.

The pressure was increasing and both teams probed more as United boss Anthony Storey rang the changes – Charlie Ball and James Stone had already joined the fray when James Hull replaced Nones. And 47 second later, Hull made it 2-0, breaking Common’s resistance completely and sending the Oval crowd home happy.

Nearly 250 braved the cold, and in a great atmosphere, football was the real winner as United prepared for Tuesday night’s visit to Bognor in the last 16 of the Sussex Senior Cup.

This Saturday Eastbourne United’s visitors are fourth-placed Guernsey, and it’s a 2pm kick-off at the Oval Arena.

#1937. ‘Exposed the world champions’: Spanish press react to England win in Nations League

10 man England secured a miraculous 3-2 win against world champions Spain in Madrid to top their Nations League group.

The Three Lions raced into a 3-0 lead at the Metropolitano Stadium, before Elliot Anderson conceded a penalty and was shown a straight red card for bringing down Lamine Yamal inside the area.

Mikel Oyarzabal scored the resulting spot-kick, and substitute Nico Williams set up a nervy finish as he slotted the ball home after a quick counter-attack.

Despite late pressure from Spain, England held on thanks to a superb double save from James Trafford, ending La Roja’s 43-game unbeaten run on a memorable night for Thomas Tuchel’s side.

Sunday’s result will go down as one of the most remarkable nights in England’s recent history, with Tuchel admitting his team reached the “highest level football-wise in all aspects of the game”.

Meanwhile, captain Harry Kane, who opened the scoring from the penalty spot at the end of the first half, said the victory was “as big as it gets” outside of a major tournament.

England entered the international break still carrying the scars of the World Cup, with Tuchel facing significant criticism for his in-game management during their semi-final defeat to Argentina.

However, victory over Spain means England have now won five of their six matches since returning from America, while Tuchel can point to having got his substitutions right as his side held on with 10 men to beat the reigning world and European champions in their own backyard.

England made the perfect start in the Spanish capital, with Declan Rice claiming post-match that, “The first 10 minutes was the best we’ve played” as Luis de La Fuente’s side struggled to live with England’s pressing.

ITV pundit and former Manchester United midfielder Roy Keane was similarly impressed by England’s intense start, describing their first-half performance as “perfect” after Kane gave the visitors a deserved lead just before the break.

Keane’s ITV colleague, Ian Wright, was particularly pleased for Arsenal right-back Ben White, who was subjected to boos during England’s 2-1 victory over Croatia but started and scored against Spain after a flowing passing move.

“Can I just say, I’m really pleased for Ben White and the way things have turned around for him. It’s just brilliant for him to get back in, and he was magnificent tonight,” Wright said.

“Not just with the goal, but he was making tackles, niggling the Spain players. I’m so pleased it’s ended that way for him.

“There was a lot to be excited about for England. They were 3-0 up and cruising against the world champions before the red kind of changed the game.”

Spanish outlet AS also heaped praise on England’s performance, declaring the result as “the biggest setback of the De la Fuente era” with Tuchel’s men “completely neutralising Spain.”

“England exposed the world champions in what represents the biggest setback of the De la Fuente era, a bitter end to a dream 2026. Goals from Kane, Konsa, and White rewarded a superior opponent,” a report in AS stated.

“Tuchel’s men had managed to cut off both of their opponents’ cables, the red and the blue, completely neutralising Spain.”

Fellow Spanish outlet MARCA also chose to celebrate England’s dominance rather than attack Spain’s performance.

“It’s better to lose against a formidable opponent like England, who dominated the match until they were reduced to ten men,” MARCA said before continuing by lavishing praise on Tuchel.

“Credit goes to Tuchel, though his performance has been questioned because he seemed afraid to be the hero in the World Cup match against Argentina. It’s been a long time since an opponent has so thoroughly dismantled Spain.”

#1936. ‘He’s better’ - Ex-Leeds United man weighs in on England’s James Trafford v Jordan Pickford debate

Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford is better than his England rival Jordan Pickford, according to ex-Whites winger Jermaine Pennant.

Trafford made a £40m move from Manchester City to Leeds in the summer transfer window and has enjoyed a stellar start to life in West Yorkshire.

He has made no secret of his desire to become England’s number one and across the last two international breaks, minutes have been shared evenly between Trafford and Everton’s Pickford.

Trafford delivered a strong showing in England’s 3-2 Nations League win over Spain last night (November 15) and Pennant believes he is now the better option for the Three Lions.

He told talkSPORT: “He’s better than Pickford. Pickford with England, when he puts on an England shirt, yes, he does great. But you always think there's a mistake in him. Whether it’s his kicking, whether it’s the ball at his feet or shot-stopping, he is good, but I just think from today's performance, Trafford has made a massive statement.

“And if you're Jordan Pickford, you're thinking, ‘oh, am I the number one now moving forward? Because that was a solid performance’.

“But for me, I just think moving forward now with the young guns, the new era, the new style of play, that I think you may have to start looking at Trafford to be the number one.”

Trafford made a particularly impressive double save in the dying embers in Madrid, enabling England to hang on and secure victory.

He will now head back to Leeds as Daniel Farke prepares his players to visit Chelsea on Saturday (November 21).

#1934. England winners and losers: Arsenal star rebuilding as Chelsea man suffers further setback

A terrific week for England ended with an away victory over Spain which Thomas Tuchel described as “like the Azteca reloaded”.

The Three Lions closed out their 2026 campaign by finishing top of their Nations League group thanks to a 2-1 win over Croatia last Thursday and then a heroic 10-man win in Madrid, 3-2, on Sunday.

While plenty of Tuchel’s players pushed their cases for further England involvement down the line, there were others who will feel less positive about the past week in terms of what it means for them.

Here, Standard Sport considers the winners and losers from England’s impressive autumn week.

Ben White has scored only 12 goals in his senior career but two have been for England, including the eventual winner in a famous win in Madrid.

Five years after his England debut, his first competitive start for his country came in Spain, and he didn’t disappoint.

The Arsenal man followed up a cameo against Croatia with one of England’s standout performances at the Estadio Metropolitano, defending robustly against Spain’s attacks down the left and then chipping in with that overlapping run and finish to make it 3-0.

Has had to field booing from sections of England fans since his return to the international fold in March after he walked away from their World Cup squad in 2022, but is rebuilding his England career successfully and will be thought of by Tuchel as one of his most well-balanced right-back options now.

Hopes to climb above Reece James and become first choice.

England’s left-back position changed hands a few times during the World Cup as Nico O’Reilly and Djed Spence battled it out mid-tournament, but that only served to make Tuchel’s decision to leave Hall behind appear all the more strange.

Hall has come back stronger and this month backed up his encouraging displays from the last international break.

Solid in the 2-1 win over Croatia, he was on another level entirely in Madrid, taking care of the threat of Lamine Yamal and finding a perfect balance between defence and attack as he helped England to victory in the world champions’ own backyard.

At the end of the last international break, when Trafford and Jordan Pickford split the four games two each, Pickford could no longer claim to be uncontested as England No1.

And after his heroics in Spain, even more so there is a debate to be had over whether it is time for England’s first-choice goalkeeper to be Leeds United’s Trafford rather than his Everton counterpart.

Pickford has never let England down in 94 caps, but Trafford made a string of stellar saves in Madrid and is eight years his junior.

Tuchel will likely continue to share the game time between them until he is pulled strongly enough in either direction. Trafford is making a very strong case for Pickford’s nine years without a genuine challenger to end with the shirt changing hands.

The Bayer Leverkusen defender has become accustomed to the bulk of his England game time being at right-back during this calendar year, but a shortage of centre-back options this month saw him start in the middle in both games

Quansah was solid for the most part but switched off in both games. And both errors were punished.

First he attempted a header back to Pickford from a Croatia corner that gifted the visitors a leveller at Wembley, then he dawdled on the ball long enough for Spain to intercept and race through; Elliot Anderson’s last-man red card and a Spain penalty followed.

Tuchel will hope he is stronger for the mistakes he made, but 23-year-old Quansah will be disappointed as he heads back to Germany.

Arguably it is harsh to include a player who was not even involved in the two matches, but the reason for Cole Palmer’s absence this month spoke volumes.

After dropping out of the last camp due to load management and being told by Tuchel that he “misses too many opportunities” to play for his country, this time the Chelsea talisman was not even selected.

Already faces huge competition in the No10 role but now there seems to be something of a repair job required if he is to get back into the fold and into Tuchel’s plans.

The 28-year-old is approaching 40 caps but his England career has been a strange old saga, really. Only Lee Carsley has ever appeared to truly trust him; Gareth Southgate and now Tuchel, less so.

Not in favour at Real Madrid under Jose Mourinho, his England game time across the autumn has felt a result of Reece James’s injuries and evidence right-back is a problem position more than it has an opportunity earned through strong club form.

Categorising Alexander-Arnold as a sublime passer who is suspect defensively became cliché long ago — yet being pinched of the ball in a poor area by Croatia was just the latest confirmation.

England managers have lacked the faith required to start him in England’s toughest matches for years now, and so it continued as he remained an unused substitute in Madrid.

White is just the latest player to climb above him in the pecking order.
